God guides one to the verification of such sciences, which discursive thoughts cannot attain and ordinary sight does not perceive.

[Editorial heading: Opening of Text Thirteen: the limit of knowledge of created things]

**Al-Mahāʾimī (introducing the next text):** This noble text explains the remaining secrets of the subject. It states the furthest attainable degree of knowledge of things other than God, and the degree of union possible with them. The utmost such union occurs in the mirror of eternal divine knowledge. Things are intrinsically different from one another; God cannot be known as He is in Himself, because what has no being of its own cannot become united with existence as such. He is unknowable from the aspect of unqualified absoluteness, for the conditioned qua conditioned cannot be united with the absolute qua absolute. Moreover, His determinations are without end, just as human states are without end. One therefore knows Him in relation to the correspondence between such states and His determinations, which are His names; knowledge of His names and intrinsic modalities is thereby conditioned. Within these limits one comes to know His decree and measure.

**Qūnawī:** Know that the highest degree of knowledge of any thing whatsoever, **except the Real**, consists in knowing it through a knowledge arising from a complete vision of it in God's knowledge. This knowledge has two signs. The first is that what you have learned frees you from having to examine it again and again in the hope of increasing your understanding. For an increase in knowledge after a prior claim to know the thing indicates that the first knowledge was deficient. Had it been perfect from the outset, further acquisition would be unnecessary, as is the case with God's knowledge. Such completeness depends upon comprehensive intellectual knowledge of the known.

**Al-Mahāʾimī (page breaks at this point):** The highest degree of knowledge available to created knowers, whether human beings or angels, concerns a thing other than the Real, whether immediately evident or reached by reasoning. To know the Real as He knows Himself is impossible, as was explained and will be explained again. One knows the thing in this highest degree when the very thing and its reality are shown within divine knowledge, through the removal of the veils between it and ... [continued on p. 154].

title: Knowing a thing by seeing it in divine knowledge
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing from p. 153):** ...your heart, with all of its receptive powers, so that the thing is disclosed fully, without its being lost to awareness by reason of annihilation (*fanāʾ*). This differs from grasping a thing through discursive definitions, which, before complete purification, are usually accompanied by mistaken imagination and corrupt fancies. That is why one sees even accomplished rational investigators disagreeing about definitions despite their exertions.

The first of the two signs that this knowledge has been attained is that the certainty acquired by tasted experience (*dhawq*), with the purity of the heart and the keenness of the soul, makes further repeated inquiry unnecessary. Such repetition might otherwise occur through reason or unveiling, even if the original discovery had been achieved by inquiry after purification and the cultivation of these capacities. The repetition cannot be needed simply to impress the knowledge upon the heart, since it is already firmly established there, and the concomitant properties of the known can be deduced from it.

An attempt to increase one's knowledge after claiming already to possess complete knowledge is possible only where the first knowledge was deficient. Were the first knowledge exhaustive in every respect, an increase would seek an aspect already possessed. This would be the impossible acquisition of what is already acquired. Since divine knowledge is perfect in every respect, its supposed increase is impossible. One may, however, speak of an articulated determination of what is already known wholly in itself, so that it comes to be referred to in detail. The kind of knowledge which renders further inquiry unnecessary depends on encompassing everything about the known; since a conditioned knower cannot encompass the unconditioned Real, this cannot occur in any creature's knowledge of God.

**Qūnawī:** The second sign indicating that this knowledge has been acquired and is sound is that the reach of one's knowledge extends throughout the thing and goes beyond its restriction, until one sees its furthest limit as connected to the absoluteness of the Real.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The second sign confirms both the acquisition of knowledge through wholly seeing the thing in God's knowledge and its validity. Unlike the first sign, which merely shows that the thing is known, this also permits knowledge of why it is so. Qūnawī says it is a sign *from which one draws an inference*: there is an evidential path here analogous to rational demonstration. It is that knowledge extends to all the thing's parts, accidental features and different respects; then it passes beyond it to what is above it, in the form of more fundamental characteristics and accidents; and in turn to what is above those, repeatedly, until the utmost horizon of the thing comes into sight ... [the argument continues on p. 155].

title: The horizon of the known and the inexhaustibility of divine manifestation
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī (continued):** ...and the conceptions of everything above it, until its furthest conceivable boundary is seen as connected with the Real's absoluteness, beyond which there is nothing. Only then is the thing known with complete knowledge. This requires seeing the thing within God's knowledge, which comprehends the beginning, the end and every intermediate connection, without limit.

The first sign has already implied that one cannot possess such complete knowledge of God, because His determinations are without end and the finite cannot encompass that which has no limit. The first passage therefore left the point implicit; here it is stated expressly.

**Qūnawī:** Knowledge of the Real is not of this sort. It attaches to Him only insofar as He becomes determined within a degree, a locus of manifestation, a state, an aspect, or a consideration. Whenever He is delimited for the knower through a determination under one of these heads, there becomes apparent and determinate to that knower, from the absolute Essence and according to the state of the recipient of disclosure, something that was not determined for that person before.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** No human knowledge of the Real can run through Him and then transcend Him in the way just described. Such knowledge concerns Him through some definite level, such as *aḥadiyya* or *wāḥidiyya*; through a manifesting locus, such as spirits or bodies; through the states of manifestation and hiddenness; through the considerations of absoluteness and restriction; or through the consideration that none of these restricts Him, without any contradiction. Each of these is a determination, whereas real absoluteness is a negative notion. At any given moment the knower receives from the absolute Essence a new determination appropriate to the state of the recipient, distinct from what was delimited previously. But where is the unconditioned absoluteness in such apprehensions? To comprehend it would require comprehending all that lay beyond an individual determination, thus conditioning the absolute by what could be conceptualized beyond it.

Qūnawī next argues that divine determinations are inexhaustible: some of them can certainly be conceived, but there is no final determination enclosing all the rest, for this is the rank of absoluteness.

**Qūnawī:** Just as the human being's states do not reach any fixed terminal boundary, so the determinations of the Real and the varieties of His manifestation to humanity are inexhaustible, occurring in proportion to human states—which themselves are determinations of the absolute Essence of the Real and varieties of His disclosure.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The writings of the people of realization have already pointed out elsewhere that the divine names are names corresponding to states, and that states succeed one another in connection with the fixed entities.

title: States, names and the impossibility of encompassing the Real
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**[Continuation of the discussion of Text Thirteen]**

**Qūnawī:** By contrast, the Real displays Himself through states, as the Most High says, “Every day He is upon some affair” (Qurʾān 55:29). Understand; do not interpret the matter away. Endeavour instead first to see it directly. Believe, submit, and you will be safe. God alone gives success and inspiration.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Human states do not reach a final state after which none is possible. Their change and succession is a matter of observation. Since they are determinations of the absolute Essence and varieties in the appearances of that Essence, the Real's determinations and modes of disclosure to human beings have no final limit. A determination differs from a variety of manifestation: the former is a cause of manifestation insofar as it is surrounded by the qualifying attributes that bring the manifestation about; the latter is the diversity of appearances occasioned by diverse determinations. Because human states and attributes constitute loci in which the Essence appears under the consideration of attributes, their diversity occasions diversity of manifestation, and each manifestation entails a determinate relation of correspondence. Human states thus serve as qualifying conditions for such differentiations. The divine names, under which the Real becomes determined, are names in relation to those human states, which mediate the diversity of manifestation and hence of determinations.

The Qurʾānic statement that He is engaged in an affair each day (55:29) has elsewhere been used to indicate that these affairs are inexhaustible: the days do not terminate, so neither do the affairs. Since the divine affairs stand in relation to the fixed entities and the comprehensive human being includes all of these, the states of the human being are likewise inexhaustible, as are the resulting varieties of manifestation and determinations. It is therefore impossible to encompass them. How, then, could one reach their furthest end and proceed beyond them to circumscribe what lies beyond? Understand. Do not reinterpret this statement away, for it is intended as stated; seek to witness it. Believe first and submit, rather than mistakenly claim to know what cannot be known, namely the Real through every one of His determinations. God grants this realization, which is the realization of the limits of knowing; He inspires surrender where attainment has been found impossible. God knows best.

**[Opening of Text Fourteen, on the same printed page.] Al-Mahāʾimī:** Qūnawī designates the following text an exalted text. The preceding discussion established that the Real is united with all things, and therefore knows them perfectly, whereas creatures cannot be united with Him in the same fashion and so cannot know Him through all His determinations, much less in absolute freedom from determination. The present text explains the majesty that both permits and veils this union. Under unconditioned absoluteness, unity so prevails that multiplicity does not appear, even though the absolute has a relation to determination. Under qualification, by contrast, there remains a relation to absoluteness, but it does not prevail: plurality is actually manifest. An apprehension of absoluteness is possible only to the degree that unity is manifest within the qualified, and it is not a knowledge of absoluteness in the manner that the Absolute knows it.

title: Every absolute has a face toward restriction
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Qūnawī:** Know that no existent described as absolute lacks an aspect toward restriction, even if only through becoming a determinate object of the thought of some thinker or several thinkers. Nor is there any existent judged to be restricted that lacks an aspect toward absoluteness. Yet none knows this except one who knows things completely, after knowing the Real and everything by which the Real is known. Whoever has not tasted this vision has not realized true knowledge of either God or creation.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Every existent describable as absolute has, without exception, some aspect toward restriction: either it already bears a determination or can bear one without being confined to it. This is the respect in which God and creation, and creatures among themselves, stand in relation to one another. The least restriction is that the absolute becomes distinguished as an object in someone's understanding. The conception of a thing requires that it be represented through a likeness by which it is distinguished from other things, whether essentially or accidentally, even at the level of a single instance. Thus the absolute is restricted in an individual's conception without ceasing to be absolute in itself; and in the conceptions of many thinkers it receives representations that are numerically distinct, especially where those representations differ from one mind to another.

Equally, anything judged to be restricted has an aspect toward absoluteness. One cannot make a judgment about the absolute without recognizing some character under which to judge it; once recognized, the character may form the apparent limitation. Yet it still has an aspect toward the absolute, because a limiting predicate inheres in something more fundamental than that predicate, to which thought can return. The bearer cannot simply be eliminated while the predicate remains, for an attribute cannot subsist without a subject. Hence the existence in every conditioned existent is the absolute, intrinsically necessary existence of the Real, which is qualified by the attributes of its loci of appearance.

Such a point can be understood only by someone who has fully known that things, considered as quiddities, do not themselves possess existence, but are encountered with existence so that it appears through the mirrors they afford and their descriptions become the qualifications of its manifestation. Nonexistent quiddities are not independently attributes of existence, for this would make what exists bear as an intrinsic attribute its contrary, nonexistence; neither are such quiddities the independently existing bearers of existence. Rather, absolute existence is the bearer, and its apparent qualifications arise through its relation to these quiddities.

title: Quiddity and existence; opening of Text Fifteen
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing Text Fourteen):** Those qualifications become manifest at the level of relation after having been undifferentiated within the absolute Essence. Their proper understanding requires knowing that the Real is absolute existence, which in turn requires knowing that He exists of Himself: He is necessary, incapable of receiving nonexistence or being transformed into it. Nor is He a mere rational concept without external reality; everything is realized through Him, whereas His reality is through Himself. There is no independent existence belonging to any other.

Whoever has not witnessed this station—that existence is absolute, that it appears under qualifications by relation to its loci, and that the quiddities have no being of their own—has not realized what it means to know the Real as absolute existence. The Real is not an accident inhering in quiddities, nor a thing whose being is conditioned by them; thus He is not multiplied or individually determined by their multiplicity. Nor do creatures possess existence by themselves: they exist through Him, and so remain, considered in themselves, upon the station of nonexistence. The Real, as He always was, has nothing independently coexistent with Him in eternity. Understand.

**[Opening of Text Fifteen, on the same printed page.]**

**Qūnawī (title):** A text explaining the secret of perfection and *greater perfection*.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The preceding text, in saying that every absolute has an aspect toward qualification, might prompt two mistaken thoughts. First, that qualification detracts from the absolute by excluding other qualifications; second, that it makes the absolute more perfect because it previously lacked that qualification. The present text addresses the first mistake by clarifying the secret of perfection and the second by clarifying the secret of the more perfect, after stating a governing distinction.

**Qūnawī:** The Real has an intrinsic perfection and a perfection of the divine names whose manifestation depends on bringing the world into being. Viewed in the light of determination, both are perfections of the names; for every judgment made by a judge concerning something presupposes that the thing judged has become determinate in the judge's conception. Were the Essence not conceived before the names were predicated of it, and distinguished from everything else through its independence in possessing existence, one could not judge it to possess intrinsic perfection. Every determination through which the Real is conceived is one of His names, since among the realizers the names are nothing but determinations of the Real. Hence every perfection predicated of the Real may, under this consideration, be called a perfection of the names. Conversely, insofar as the emanation of the divine names from the presence of His unity is an entailment of His Essence, all the perfections predicated of Him are intrinsic.

title: Three accounts of intrinsic and nominal perfection
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The perfection inseparable from the Real may be considered in three ways. In the first, it is divided into intrinsic and nominal perfection. Intrinsic perfection is that whose existence and manifestation depend on nothing: it is eternally and perpetually manifest to the Essence in the Essence, without dependence on determinations or restrictions, for the Real is independent of all worlds. The existence of nominal perfection, on the other hand, likewise depends on nothing, but its manifestation and actual expression depend on the world's coming to exist, because the names express relations between Essence and things and a relation is not manifested without its terms. This does not mean that the Essence gains a perfection it lacked; rather, after its perfect manifestation to itself, it manifests within distinct loci.

Under a second consideration, both are perfections of the names: to judge that the Real possesses perfection, one must first conceive what is being judged. Such a conception distinguishes the subject from what lies outside it, however slightly—even, for example, through our conceiving it before the names are attributed to it or through our distinguishing its independence in the possession of existence. Anything distinguished in relation to something else is in that respect determined. Every determination through which the Real is conceived is called a divine name among the realizers, for names are, considered as bare relations, non-existent in themselves and cannot be independent causes of existence. They are in truth determinations of the Real under such relations. Thus there is no predication of perfection without some determination, and both modes of perfection may be called nominal, even when their manifestation does not depend on bringing anything else into existence.

Under a third consideration, both perfections are intrinsic. Those called intrinsic under the first consideration are plainly so. The others also spring from the presence of divine unity. Unity gives rise to the perspectives of oneness and all-encompassing unity, and the names proceed from the latter. What arises from something which itself arises from the Essence ultimately arises from the Essence. Moreover, its being made manifest is already included in what the Essence entails, for the names are enfolded within it. Hence all the perfections ascribed to the Real may be ascribed to His Essence under this consideration. Understand.

**Qūnawī:** When this has been settled, we say that one whose perfection is from his own Essence cannot be diminished in that perfection by outward accidents and concomitant features in certain levels of manifestation—as though these could undermine it.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** This addresses the first apparent difficulty. Perfection that belongs to a thing essentially is its perfection eternally. It is not impaired when, relative to a level or a manifesting locus, it is accompanied by contingent and passing restrictions or by externally associated, more persistent concomitants. Even when those qualifications exclude other or opposite qualifications, they cannot damage intrinsic perfection ... [continued p. 160].

title: Qualification neither diminishes nor adds to the divine Essence
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī (continued):** ...because an attribute attaches to the Real under the consideration of a particular level, not at every other level. He thus remains absolute and, as absolute, perfect. In the first distinction, which separates intrinsic from nominal perfection, the Essence is not altered as names vary any more than it is multiplied by their multiplicity. A particular name's absence at a given level entails no deficiency in the absolute Essence. In the second account, where all perfections are regarded as nominal, every perfection remains in the first determination even if it is not manifest in later determinations; what is absent in one rank is not thereby absent from another. In the third, where all are intrinsic, the Essence is the source of every rank: the source of the first is thereby the source of what proceeds from it, and ultimately the source of all perfections. Understand.

**Qūnawī:** Nor is it permissible to imagine that its perfection contains a deficiency that is then made good by such attributes. Rather, in certain levels, external accidents and concomitants can make apparent the quality of its *greater perfection*; knowledge that this is its manner is itself among those excellences.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** This resolves the second difficulty. Qualification does not perfect an Absolute that had previously been defective. Essential perfection remains as it always was, while a description of greater perfection becomes manifest, by means of qualifications and concomitants, at levels such as that of the Perfect Human, where divine names appear. This follows readily if intrinsic and nominal perfections are distinguished. If all perfections are called nominal, the perfection belonging to the first determination is unchanged; the additional description of greater perfection belongs to further determinations. And if all are called intrinsic, what belongs to the Essence without mediation remains unchanged, while there is an additional manifestation through intermediaries.

An objection might arise: does this not, after all, make the Essence complete itself through these manifestations? No. The quality of greater perfection appears by the manifestation of the Essence in its own affairs or modalities (*shuʾūn*). These modalities are included within the Essence and already known and present there; therefore they gain no perfection that was previously absent. What is added is only the relation of their appearing in manifesting loci, and a relation, as such, is not another independently existing perfection. The author mentions knowledge of this state because, in the rank of absoluteness, these affairs are not differentiated but remain enfolded or potential; one cannot ascribe to what is merely potential the completed appearance belonging to the level of determination.

**[Opening of Text Sixteen on the same printed page.] Al-Mahāʾimī:** Qūnawī calls the next text a very noble text. Having just examined perfection, which is a *description*, he must now consider what is described, as it is known through its true levels. It is noble because it comprehends all the realities described as perfect, and exceedingly noble because it makes possible complete understanding of the described realities along with their attributes.

title: The Reality knows Himself without an additional image
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**[Text Sixteen, after the introduction translated on p. 160.]**

**Qūnawī:** The reality of the Real consists of the form of His knowledge of Himself, inasmuch as that knowledge is determined through its relation to Himself, under the consideration in which knowledge, the knower and the known are one.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** What essentially distinguishes the Real from everything else is the form of His knowledge of Himself. Were such a form hypothetically distinct from what it represents, it would correspond perfectly to it. Here, however, the point is the necessary self-relation of knowledge entailed by His conception of Himself. This excludes consideration of God's self-knowledge through His appearance in the loci of manifestation, or through the conception other knowers possess of Him. Nor does His knowledge of Himself involve an added intelligible image standing over against a separately existing subject, with another relation joining them. Such an image would veil the known, and God is exalted above this. It would also introduce multiplicity into the first determination, which is simple from every point of view. Rather, knowing, knower and known are one, because neither the image nor its relation adds something to what is imaged. This excludes the differentiated self-knowledge ascribed under the degree of the names.

**Qūnawī:** His intrinsic attribute, which is not other than His Essence, is a unicity of comprehensiveness—an all-gathering oneness beyond which no gathering, relation or consideration can be conceived.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Qūnawī mentions the intrinsic attribute because it is through such an attribute that the Essence is known to the highest degree available to the knower. It is not other than the Essence in what it refers to, even if the concepts of subject and attribute differ. Without conceptual difference there could be no meaningful predication of an attribute of a subject. The intrinsic attribute is the unique comprehension of existence and all its ranks and descriptions. Nothing more comprehensive can be conceived, for it comprehends both unity as distinguished from differentiation and unity as gathering differentiation, without either opposing the other or restricting the comprehensiveness to one side. There is no special relation confining it to gathering rather than differentiation, nor an unqualified absoluteness superadded to it as a further consideration. It comprehends both the unrestricted and the conditioned without being confined by the very description of comprehending them.

**Qūnawī:** Actual realization of this attribute through witnessing, and complete knowledge of it, consist in knowing that in every determinate thing the Real may be judged determinate according to what makes Him apprehensible in it under determination, while also knowing that He is not confined by that determination and that, considered as He is in Himself, He is undetermined.

title: The Real as known in loci of manifestation
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī:** To witness this attribute truly, so that one's seeing amounts to the eye or reality of certainty, and to know it completely with the certainty of knowledge, is to recognize the Real in every thing determined as a rank, a branch, or an individual. One may judge the Real determinate in that thing, not because His Essence is intrinsically limited, but because the senses or intellect, or His self-disclosure under names proper to the rank, make Him apprehensible there in a particular manner. The witness must know that He is not restricted by determination at all, much less by the particular determination presently encountered; considered in Himself He is not determined. His appearing in different forms depends on ranks. He therefore retains the purity of His absoluteness while appearing in a determinate locus. To know this is to know an all-embracing unity beyond which no other union, relation or consideration can be placed. Since the attribute had been declared identical in reality with the Essence, Qūnawī now explains this identification.

**Qūnawī:** This is the form of His knowledge of Himself. Thus He knows His Essence as determinate relative to His manifestation in things according to those things, and relative to one who witnesses Him only in a locus; yet He also knows, exalted is He, that considered in Himself He is undetermined, even at the very moment when He is judged determinate, because the apprehension of one who perceives Him only through a locus is limited—whether that locus is regarded as the very reality appearing or as other than it.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** God's being present in each determinate thing in a way that warrants judgment about His appearance there—while not being confined to it and while remaining undetermined in Himself—is what the form of divine self-knowledge signifies. If such a form were an addition, it would perfectly correspond to His reality. In divine self-knowledge the Essence is understood as determinate relative to its appearances in the determinate things, in proportion to their receptive aptitudes, without thereby becoming confined by them. It is also known in relation to the one who sees it only in a locus. Such a person's knowledge is a shadowed participation in divine knowledge as it relates to that person's fixed entity. But God knows, under another consideration not restricted to this relational knowledge, that He is Himself undetermined, even when a creature judges Him determined. This further consideration is not the very same as God's knowing Himself in connection with that limited knower, because a knowledge of something follows what its object is; only the creature perceiving Him under a particular limitation knows Him through that limitation alone. And this holds whether that person takes the locus to be identical with what appears or regards it as something other than what appears ... [continued on p. 163].

title: Divine reality and the essential poverty of creation
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī (continued):** ...In either case the Real knows the person under the aspect of that person's conception of Him, whether the conception is gravely mistaken or true in one respect; and in another aspect He knows Himself as unqualified by that person's conception. Consider this.

**Qūnawī:** The reality of creation consists in the form of their Lord's knowledge of them; their intrinsic quality is *poverty*, which makes manifest absolute richness—but not just any sort of poverty. Understand.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The essential reality distinguishing creatures from the Real, despite the unity of existence, is their form as known in their Lord's knowledge at the second determination. These are the fixed entities (*aʿyān thābita*), not the undifferentiated intrinsic modalities (*shuʾūn*). This is the reality of the fixed entities, not an independently self-subsisting reality of created beings. The intrinsic quality entailed by their nature without mediation is dependence on God: dependence upon Him for the establishment of their intelligible realities in His knowledge, for the existence that appears through them, and for the qualities by which they are known. Such dependence gives expression to the unrestricted self-sufficiency of the Real. The poverty of which Qūnawī speaks is the poverty whose recognition brings to light divine richness; not every species of dependence is the intrinsic quality of creation. For example, the divine names' dependence upon loci for their manifestation is not itself that same creaturely poverty. Understand.

**[Opening of Text Seventeen on the same printed page.] Al-Mahāʾimī:** The following text is called exceedingly noble because the preceding teaching, that the Real's manifestation follows the receptive character of the loci, could suggest He lacks true essential attributes—contrary to reason, transmitted revelation and consensus. The new text therefore examines transcendence or incomparability (*tanzīh*) in its different formulations, identifying what is sound in them. Its nobility lies in joining incomparability and resemblance while affirming every perfection of God without making other things partners with Him, and in declaring Him beyond all descriptions. The resulting insight is deeper than unaided rational understanding or the surface of revealed wording.

**Qūnawī:** The fruit of rational incomparability is to distinguish the Real from what is called other than Him through negative attributes, out of concern for imagined deficiencies that are posited in minds but do not occur in existence. The fruit of scripturally expressed incomparability is to deny existential plurality and partnership in the rank of divinity, even as Scripture affirms a sharing in certain positive attributes without equality or likeness. [The illustrations continue on p. 164.]

title: The inadequacy of purely negative transcendence
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**[Qūnawī's Qurʾānic illustrations, continued:]** God is described as the best of providers (Qurʾān 62:11), the best of creators (23:14), the most merciful of those who show mercy (7:151), and greater than anything that can be compared with Him (cf. 9:72), and similarly elsewhere.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** God is declared incomparable through reason, revealed law and unveiling, but their modes of incomparability are not the same. Reason exempts Him from certain features because it regards them as deficiencies. By excluding these, reason attributes to Him negative qualifications opposite to them. The rational procedure thus distinguishes the Real from other things by such negations. Qūnawī does not accept this result as sufficient: deficiencies, as deficiencies, are privative considerations and cannot belong to existence in itself. Everything that actually exists has perfection insofar as it exists. Deficiency is posited by the understanding when a manifestation occurs in one locus rather than another. Nor is there contradiction within existence as such; opposition belongs to comparisons between definite ranks.

The author calls this the *fruit* rather than the true content of rational incomparability, because he does not accept the idea that God's distinction from all other things consists of His possessing attributes that they lack, or their possessing attributes excluded from Him. This would prevent the Real from embracing all perfections and would fail to establish the most complete unity.

As for the incomparability communicated by the outward sense of Scripture, the expressions of the Book, the Sunna and the public statements of learned authorities exclude a partner, equal or like in the rank of divinity. Its consequence is the denial of several independently existing gods. Qūnawī specifies existential plurality rather than merely conceptual plurality. Yet even this is not the whole matter, for revealed speech also attributes such positive perfections as hearing, seeing, life, knowledge, power, will and speech to creatures, without equating them with divine attributes. The denial of likeness does not abolish attribution of the same general terms under unequal modes. In speaking of God as the *best* of providers and creators, and the most merciful of the merciful, Scripture itself retains a grammatical comparison with other providers and merciful agents. The surface reading, taken to deny all commonality whatsoever, is therefore incomplete; a fuller understanding must reconcile the scriptural expressions. That is the work of the incomparability disclosed through unveiling (*kashf*).

**Qūnawī (opening of the account of unveiled incomparability):** The incomparability understood by the people of unveiling is to affirm the Real's universal comprehensiveness without limiting Him to the description of comprehending; it distinguishes the rulings proper to the various divine names. Not every ruling may rightly be attributed to every name. Indeed, among the names are some to which a certain ruling cannot possibly belong, though it belongs to others. [Continued p. 165.]

title: Incomparability through unveiled comprehensiveness
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Qūnawī:** The same applies to divine attributes. Among the fruits of unveiled incomparability is the denial of any independently existing 'other' while retaining the numerical rulings that distinguish one appearance from another. This involves no positing of a deficiency that must be negated, nor conceiving a perfection that needs to be added to the Real through some further affirmation. Peace.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Here the author states the very principle of incomparability rather than merely its consequence, signalling that this mode of transcendence, unlike the preceding conceptions, is valid from the outset. Under unveiled incomparability, nothing is excluded from the Reality's comprehensiveness; yet that comprehensiveness does not enclose or delimit Him. He is present in differentiation as well as in unity. The Real thus has a unity comprehending both gathering and distinction, taken together and separately. This concerns the Essence.

For the names, unveiled incomparability means not attributing to one name every ruling that applies to another. Certain rulings cannot belong to a name *qua* that name, even though they belong to another. The Essence comprehends them all: the rulings of the name that abases cannot, *as such*, be assigned to the name that exalts, and vice versa. Qūnawī therefore makes the authentic principle and its fruit explicit. The negation of a separate 'other' follows from comprehensiveness, while the numerical distinction of appearances remains. Were every numerical distinction simply erased, differentiation would have no place and the Real would be confined to pure gathering. Thus what is called other than Him under one consideration is not independent of Him under another.

Nor does this imply an original deficiency in the Essence that is overcome by including all things. All their possibilities are comprehended there, so the Essence is not deficient; no new event alters it. Similarly, one cannot suppose that the Real acquires a perfection through some newly affirmed creaturely attribute. The Real is essentially perfect, and the perfections displayed under restriction belong in reality to Him as the ground of their manifestation.

The author's concluding expression 'peace' may be read as a salutation of those who practise this unveiled incomparability and avoid the limitation of the earlier viewpoints. Thus the Qurʾānic conclusion is appropriate: 'Glory be to your Lord, Lord of might, beyond what they describe' (37:180), for creatures' formulations of incomparability and resemblance do not exhaust Him; 'peace be upon the messengers' (37:181), because of the correctness of the transcendence they convey; and 'praise be to God, Lord of the worlds' (37:182), for He comprehends the whole without diminution or change and all perfections belong to Him. Understand.

title: Text Eighteen: The locus governs the mode of indwelling
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Qūnawī:** A noble text.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** In the preceding text it was said that all things subsist in the Real, although the Eternal cannot be the receptive locus of originated events. Earlier, it had been said that the Real pervades all things, although the Eternal is too exalted to be contained in the originated. This noble text removes that apparent difficulty, since it explains how something originated may be described as eternal under one consideration, and how the Eternal may be described as newly appearing under another. The preceding statement, that every absolute reality has an aspect toward determination and vice versa, is not thereby overturned.

**Qūnawī:** The manner in which anything is in something else follows the character of its locus, whether that locus is intelligible or formal. Consequently, the possible objects of knowledge, insofar as their determinations are established and inscribed in the knowledge of the Real, are described as pre-eternal. Likewise, everything determined in divine knowledge bears, under another aspect, the ruling of origination: the existence of the world and the knowledge possessed by its inhabitants are originated and receptive, unlike the existence and knowledge of the Real. Know this, and, if God wills, you will be rightly guided.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The establishment of any state in a locus is qualified as originated or pre-eternal in accordance with the locus, even if considered in itself that state would not be so qualified. This is true whether the locus is intelligible, such as the Creator's knowledge or created intellects, or formal, as in elemental bodies.

The possible objects of knowledge are originated by their own nature. Nevertheless, they are described as pre-eternal insofar as their determinations subsist in the eternal divine knowledge: what is established in that knowledge as an object of knowledge is not something temporally superadded to it. One must not make divine knowledge a place in which new events come to be. The same determined objects, which are described as eternal insofar as they are known by God, are subject to the ruling of origination insofar as they exist externally. The being of the cosmos and the knowledge of its inhabitants are originated in their outward existence, for they are receptive of and dependent on God's existence and knowledge.

This is not the case with the existence and knowledge of the Real, which are eternal considered in themselves. When originated things appear, the ancient existence and knowledge may be described as newly appearing **with respect to manifestation and relation**, not through an origination in themselves. The Eternal is related to the originated and thus receives a relative description without changing in His own reality. Understand this and you will reconcile the outward law (*sharīʿa*) and the inner reality (*ḥaqīqa*) at the point from which pure divine unity proceeds, if God wills.

title: Text Nineteen: Why the absolute cannot be named as though it were another thing
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Qūnawī:** A noble text, among the noblest, most majestic and most comprehensive statements of the universal principles of divine and cosmic knowledge.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The preceding text examined a thing under the aspect of the locus in which it is established; the present text considers what belongs to it under the aspect of itself. It discusses the divine realities: the Essence, its essential names and their rulings, its essential efficacy and being effective, its knowledge and its unity; the way its knowledge acts as a mirror of the Essence and names and as the source of multiplicity; and the ranks, their relations and the arising of some from others. The text is noble because it gathers the results of the previous texts, majestic because it includes their premises, and comprehensive because it unites beginnings and ends.

**Qūnawī:** Know that the application of the name *Essence* (*dhāt*) is true of the Real only in respect of His determination: that first determination which, in the conception of creatures other than the perfected, comes after an imagined absoluteness whose nature is unknown and which has no name. That supposed absoluteness is a negative description of the Essence, imagined as distinct from every determination. The affirmative reality actually given, however, is the first determination.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Beginners in this discipline sometimes suppose that the name *Essence* belongs to the Real under the aspect of sheer absoluteness. But this absoluteness is a negative meaning, without a known attribute or a name. They call it the unseen of the Real because, according to their supposition, it stands above everything. If *Essence* named something below this absoluteness, the absoluteness would be above the divine Essence; yet all agree that nothing is above Him.

The supposition derives from the reasoning that every determination is preceded by non-determination, and that non-determination is absoluteness. Qūnawī corrects it. The word *Essence* signifies the Real under consideration of the first determination, since there is, by agreement, no name preceding it. To make *Essence* the name of something prior to that determination contradicts the very assertion that the supposed prior absoluteness is not circumscribed by being an essence, just as it is not circumscribed by any description. Moreover, the Real's intelligible determination in His knowledge of Himself is considered at the first determination: what has not been conceived under that aspect by the Real cannot be conceived as something superordinate by another knower, so that the name *Essence* could be applied to it.

What the unperfected understand as a prior absoluteness is thus a mental supposition formed by contrast with various modes of absoluteness and restriction. It is a negative description, not another entity higher than the Real. Something can stand above another only if it is itself something. If one objects that it must be something because it is distinguished from all determination, the answer is that the distinction is imposed by imagination; it places an imagined non-determination above every real determination. [The argument continues on p. 168.]

title: First determination, essential names and the two presences
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** Non-determination is a negative consideration and therefore cannot genuinely be above or prior to what is determined. The first determination alone is the affirmative reality at issue. Accordingly, *the divine Essence* is a name applied there, not a name for a non-existent abstraction. Certainly one may describe the Essence negatively as not confined by either absoluteness or restriction. That is an account relative to the ranks, not an additional state prior to the first determination. Because it commonly figures in ordinary people's conception, they imagine it to precede that first determination. Understand.

**Qūnawī:** The Essence intrinsically comprehends the essential names, the keys of the unseen; and the referent of the name *Essence* is in no respect other than its names. The names, however, differ from and oppose one another; and again they are united with one another from the standpoint of the Essence that comprehends them all.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The first determination intrinsically includes the essential names, the keys of the unseen and of the divine relations: the Living, the Knowing, the Powerful, the Willing, the Hearing, the Seeing and the Speaking. Were these names present only through a further intermediary, that intermediary, rather than the essential names themselves, would be the key of the unseen.

An objection might be raised: if the first determination included several names, it would no longer be the first determination but already the presence of the names. The answer is that in the first presence the One named by the term *Essence* differs in no respect from His names. In their own presence, the second determination, the names differ conceptually from one another, sometimes oppose one another in their rulings, and also agree in the comprehending Essence. Thus they may be predicated of one another in one respect and all of them predicated of the Essence. Unity at the first determination is not equivalent to the abolition of the names; nor is their differentiation at the second equivalent to a plurality of independent essences.

**Qūnawī:** Unicity (*aḥadiyya*) describes the determination, not an absolutely unqualified something supposed to be determined, since what is absolutely unqualified has no name and no attribute.

*Editorial note:* An explanatory footnote to *aḥadiyya* is present in the online transcription but is not represented here as part of Qūnawī's or al-Mahāʾimī's running medieval text. The argument continues on p. 169.

title: Aḥadiyya, wāḥidiyya, and efficacy without a separate intermediary
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī:** This anticipates an objection. How can the Essence include the essential realities expressed by the names if it is called *Essence* at its first determination, when only the Essence alone can be conceived? Is it not called unicity precisely because the names are not distinguished there? How, then, can it comprehend them under that aspect?

Qūnawī's reply is that absolute indetermination, as such, does not become determined and has neither name nor attribute. Hence it cannot itself be described as determination or unicity. In the consideration of *aḥadiyya* the names are not distinguished; in that of *wāḥidiyya* the names are taken into account. Yet the Essence is more comprehensive than the descriptions of it as either unicity or unitive plurality, and can therefore comprehend the names without their becoming separately distinguished in the first consideration. Understand.

**Qūnawī:** From the standpoint of these names, insofar as the Essence does not differ from them, we say that the Real acts by the Essence. Understand.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** This follows from the names' non-otherness in relation to the Essence. The realized knowers can therefore say that the Essence effects things without an intermediary. On the other hand, the Essence considered solely in itself is self-sufficient beyond the worlds, so the operation of the names must also be acknowledged. Yet those names are the very Essence at the rank of unicity, and are included by the Essence at the rank of *wāḥidiyya*. Under the former respect and in their actual referent, what appears to be an intermediary is not a second entity standing between the Essence and its effect. Qūnawī's injunction to understand indicates that those who speak of an intermediary also speak truly, but under a different consideration.

**Qūnawī:** The Essence has just one inseparable concomitant, different from it only relationally; that concomitant is knowledge.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Consider the seven essential names. The Essence has one first concomitant, whether approached under the aspect of *aḥadiyya* or of *wāḥidiyya*; the others follow through it, in the order of intelligible dependence. Even this first concomitant is not really separate from the Essence. Under the differentiated aspect of *wāḥidiyya* it is distinct only by relation, and under unicity the knower, knowledge and known are united from every aspect. Thus what might be spoken of as an intermediary between Essence and the other essential names is not an intermediary in any fully independent sense.

Qūnawī specifies *knowledge*, rather than *life*, as the immediate concomitant. Knowledge conceptually presupposes life, but life is itself cognized through knowledge. The dependence in view is therefore one of conception rather than temporal production. [Continued p. 170.]

title: The one concomitant, unitive plurality and knowledge as mirror
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** All these essential attributes are eternal and everlasting. No temporal sequence is intended by the order in which one is comprehended through another.

**Qūnawī:** The Real's unitive oneness (*waḥdāniyya*) is established in respect of knowledge. In it and through it the rank of divinity and the other ranks and things known become determined, for all are inscribed therein.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Unitive oneness follows the Essence's comprehension of the names, but it is established under consideration of knowledge, because knowledge receives all the intelligible determinations and nothing is thus determined prior to being known in that way. In knowledge and through knowledge the degree of divinity, which is *wāḥidiyya*, becomes determined, as do the other universal ranks and particular objects of knowledge. Qūnawī says both *in it* and *through it* to indicate that determination is a ruling about a determinate object: the intelligible inscription within knowledge is the occasion of that determination, much as it is with the other ranks. Furthermore, what contains all in knowledge encompasses them; what is encompassed is lower in rank than its comprehending principle, and what is lower subsists through what is higher.

**Qūnawī:** Knowledge is the mirror of the Essence insofar as the Essence comprises the essential names from which it differs in no respect, as already explained. Knowledge is also the source and the spring from which intelligible multiplicity proceeds. I called knowledge a mirror for the known things, and a mirror for the Essence with its essential names, because knowledge, insofar as it is distinguished from the Essence by a conceptual rather than a real distinction, makes the Real's determination conceivable in His understanding of Himself within Himself. Thus His intrinsic knowledge is like a mirror for Him.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Knowledge is the place of the intelligible inscription of all because it mirrors the Essence together with its essential names. Those names are the keys of the unseen; for the Essence to encompass them is to encompass all its intrinsic modes (*shuʾūn*). The Essence appears in the first rank with the essential names precisely because they are not other than it. Its appearance is their appearance.

The modes do not yet appear as distinct in that rank, because their discrimination depends on the discrimination of the names. Although the names appear through the appearance of the Essence, they are not yet differentiated in the first determination. Knowledge, however, mirrors the Essence with those names, and for that reason is the origin and emergence-point of intelligible multiplicity: the distinct meanings represented by the fixed entities. Through it those entities proceed, as intelligibly differentiated, from the first rank and are manifest in the second.

An objection arises: how can knowledge be a *mirror* of the Essence if the essential names are not other than it and knowledge itself is not other than the Essence? A mirror ordinarily differs from what it displays. Qūnawī answers that the analogy depends only upon a relative or conceptual distinction, not an actual ontological division. [Continued p. 171.]

title: Knowledge, self-manifestation and the universal ranks
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** When one says that knowledge is the mirror of the Essence, the operative term is *like* a mirror. It would be impossible for a thing to depend on itself as on an independent second thing. What makes the expression legitimate is the relative intelligible distinction between divine knowledge and the Essence at the second consideration, the distinction made possible by considering the Essence's relation of understanding itself. Through that merely conceptual difference the Real's determination in His self-understanding can be conceived. His very Self is like a mirror for His Self, and since His knowledge is His Self, His intrinsic knowledge may all the more appropriately be called His mirror.

**Qūnawī:** For this reason we said elsewhere that the reality of the Real is the form of His knowledge of Himself. We also indicated that every manifest thing appearing in a locus differs from that locus in one or more respects, except the Real, who may be the very manifest and the very locus of manifestation. Remember.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** This recalls the treatment of the Real's self-knowledge earlier in the work. Knowledge may be likened to the mirror of the Essence because its difference is relational and conceptual rather than real. Without some analogy of a reflected form one could not say that His knowledge contains a form of Himself; yet the analogy must not be literalized. There is no real form imprinted over against Him, because the knowing and the known are not two entities and actual multiplicity does not obtain in the first rank.

Qūnawī previously showed the absence of real difference between the knower and known by showing that not everything called a manifestation produces a separate entity alongside its source. He also explained the authentic unity which removes the predicates and relations that would divide it, and connected that unity with the Real's self-understanding in His determination. This is the exception to the ordinary rule: where created things are concerned, what appears is distinct from its locus under at least one aspect; in the unique case of the Real the manifest and the locus can be the same Reality. The reader is asked to remember the different earlier discussions in order to understand the exception correctly.

**Qūnawī:** As for the *ranks* (*marātib*), they are universal determinations encompassed by the single intrinsic concomitant, knowledge. They are like loci passed through by the unrestricted effusion issuing from the Essence, considering the non-otherness of the effusion and its giver, as previously noted in connection with the Real's being manifest and being a locus of manifestation.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The ranks are universal determinations, and universals insofar as they are universal have their being in knowledge. Knowledge, the one intrinsic concomitant, therefore comprehends the ranks. They are inscribed therein just as the Essence is mirrored therein, though their two kinds of inscription must not be confused. The ranks have their distinct forms in the presence of knowledge, and in that sense are like the places through which the universal effusion passes. These forms qualify the effusion according to the receptivities of the ranks. [Continued p. 172.]

title: The universal ranks modify one unrestricted effusion
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing from p. 171):** The universal effusion from the Essence, in passing through the intelligible ranks, is delimited by the particular capacities of those ranks. It is called unrestricted because the manifest and the locus of manifestation are united at the first determination, the rank of unity. Here the source of the effusion is the manifest Reality, and the effusion is what constitutes the appearance through its locus; at that level, they are not two independent things. The effusion is qualified only through the additional forms that belong to the ranks as they are inscribed in the divine knowledge.

**Qūnawī:** The ranks have a share in the reality of producing an effect, though not absolutely: they do so insofar as they are, as I have said, like loci.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Since the effusion becomes differentiated as it traverses the ranks, they contribute to its effective determination. The single unrestricted effusion is qualified and multiplied by the differentiated loci; before these considerations there is no such qualification, because effusion and giver are considered one. But the ranks do not exercise efficacy absolutely. As was shown in an earlier text, a thing is an agent in the fullest sense only if it is effective as that very thing, without having to introduce an additional qualification or some external excellence. In the present case, the rank's effect depends precisely on the addition of its function as an intelligible locus. This is a qualified, not absolutely independent, causality.

**Qūnawī:** Every rank is therefore an intelligible place of disclosure for a group of rulings of existence and possibility. Those rulings branch from the essential names, from the principal divine names, and from the derivative names which follow them.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Each rank is an intelligible mirror for the rulings of necessity and possibility, much as a receptacle displays the colour of what it contains: one says that water takes on the colour of its vessel. The rulings of necessity concern effective agency; those of possibility concern receptivity. The two kinds are joined in each rank without being simply identical. The former branch from the essential names that do not signify realities added to the Essence—for instance the names *He*, *God*, *Existence*, *Pre-eternal*, *All-knowing*, and *Manifest*. They also branch from the mothers of the divine names, that is, the primary names previously described as the keys of the unseen. The rulings of possibility branch from the following or derivative names, such as Creator, Provider and Fashioner, in their connections to the receptivities of creatures. It is through the rulings of these names that the ranks have the efficacy being discussed. In ultimate truth the efficacious source is the names, and hence the Essence to which they belong. Understand.

**Qūnawī (opening of the next sentence):** The ranks have fixed entities in the domain of divine knowledge and intelligible apprehension, and ... [continued p. 173].

title: Fixed entities have no independent efficacy
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Qūnawī (continuing):** ...they do not exercise an effect independently, but only through existence. Such too is the relation of the rulings of necessity to the ranks: these rulings are effective, and their effects appear in all that is related to a rank and becomes determined there, through the conditioning of unrestricted effusion as it reaches and passes through the rank.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The text explicitly repeats that it is **the ranks**, not the previously mentioned names, that have fixed entities, lest the pronoun be taken as referring to the nearest antecedent. Their mode of efficacy is that of intelligible loci of the combined rulings of necessity and possibility. The fixed entities considered as intelligible forms are, under that respect, non-existent externally; the non-existent does not act upon what exists. The qualified effusion, however, is existential and realized externally. Thus the fixed entities possess no independent power to produce it. Their effect is through existence, which carries the rulings of necessity through the essential names, and the rulings of possibility through the derivative names.

Why, then, does Qūnawī not simply attribute the entire effect to existence? Because existence as unrestricted does not, by itself and as unqualified, account for the variety of its concrete appearances. Considered in its unity, the effusion is one; its differentiation depends on the ranks. Their rulings appear in every effusion that relates to them. The relation called 'contact' is not a physical collision. It is the effect's becoming determined at a rank, according to that rank's capacity. An effusion that **arrives and remains** at a rank is conditioned in one manner, whereas an effusion **passing through** it toward another rank is conditioned in another manner. These differences account for why ranks may have an effect even when a disclosure is not arrested within them.

Nor is it enough to give this efficacy exclusively to the rulings of necessity and possibility. Those rulings do not stand alone; they have to be established under the ranks. The resulting causal account therefore considers the intelligible ranks together with the relevant divine and possible rulings. Understand.

**Qūnawī:** The ranks are like relative endpoints when one considers the course of essential effusion and existential self-disclosure through the stations and degrees determined between eternity without beginning and eternity without end—without a final goal or fixed resting-place.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** This answers an objection. If ranks influence effusion only when effusion reaches and is determined at them, how can they condition what merely passes through them? Because each rank is a **relative limit** in relation to a disclosure's course, whether the disclosure remains there or continues through it. The commentary continues on p. 174.

title: Relative termini, perpetual self-disclosure and renewed creation
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** A rank may serve as the relative endpoint for the effusion that sustains its own existence through the whole duration allotted to it, as in the case of sanctified spirits. Or it may be a relative endpoint for an effusion that passes onward to other ranks. Even where the special share proper to that rank does not leave it, the effusion proceeds through it toward things below it in rank and acts upon them. For that reason every rank is a relative destination: at each, what reaches it becomes determinate according to its capacity.

The ranks are relative endpoints by reference to the journey of essential effusion, that is, existential self-disclosure, through successive stations and degrees. The term *stations* may be applied to those points from which the effusion moves altogether to another place; *degrees* to the remaining differences of order, including those in which a disclosure endures while another proceeds. The series is situated between what is without beginning and what is without end, yet there is no last goal beyond which nothing remains, and no absolute cessation at the point already reached. New creation (*khalq jadīd*) is constantly realized across the instances of manifestation. Movement is treated here as an affirmative existential event, whereas rest, insofar as it is the sheer negation of movement, is privative. Consequently the course of disclosure is ceaseless. A rank thus counts as the end of what has preceded it, but not as the absolute end of what succeeds it. Understand.

**Qūnawī:** It is now evident from what I have explained that the ranks gather the groups of rulings that stand established within them from the presences of necessity and possibility. They make manifest the results of their conjunction, but according to the ranks themselves—not simply according to the rulings taken alone, nor according to unrestricted effusion alone. Their relation is that of shapes and moulds to things shaped and moulded when these reach and occupy them. This is their efficacy. They are fixed in their intelligible entities; the resulting rulings are traced back to them and ultimately attributed to them, for they are their source and their return. Understand.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** A rank gathers the rulings of necessity and possibility that apply to it, and these remain established relative to it, even if a particular effusion passes away from it or affects something else through it. The rulings arise from the divine and necessary names and from the names connected with the possible realm, whose respective presences abide. Accordingly the rulings derived from them also have a stable intelligible place.

The ranks manifest the results produced by the conjunction of the two orders of rulings. The manifestation is ascribed to the rank as the intelligible mirror and place of conjunction, not to the rulings taken in abstraction: without their place of establishment they are not independent agents. Nor can it be attributed merely to unrestricted effusion, which, as such, does not independently produce its own differentiation. This is clarified by comparing a rank with a shape or mould: the arriving effusion receives a determinate form, while the mould, under the relevant consideration, stays as it is. [Continued p. 175.]

title: The fixed entities, responsibility and the order of the names
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** The fixed entities of the ranks remain established in the domain of knowledge. The results of the assembled rulings are referred to them, since the effects are the effects of those intelligible realities; the difference of outcomes follows from the difference of the fixed entities. Consequently the variation of recompense is connected with the determinate recipients and their acts, not with a wholly undifferentiated divine command considered in isolation. These determinate entities are the sites where recompense occurs, while necessity and its rulings do not, by themselves, become recipients of reward or punishment. The ranks are also the points from which the relevant actions proceed. The Qurʾānic expression 'as a recompense for what they used to do' states this relationship. None of this implies that the fixed entities have existence independently of God; their existence is through Him and His self-disclosure. Understand: the point enables the joining of divine determination (*qadar*) and revealed obligation (*sharʿ*).

**Qūnawī:** Then know that the ranks are linked by the emergence of some from others, and the names are likewise ordered. Divinity, together with its universal names—the Living, the Knowing, the Powerful and the Willing—is a shadow of the Essence insofar as the Essence intrinsically comprises the keys of the unseen. Yet between divinity and the Essence under that aspect there is a subtle difference, disclosed to the perfected in their direct experience. In the divine presence the degree of divinity is conceived as distinct from the principal names just mentioned. The Essence, however, is conceived as different from its essential names only by those veiled from essential self-disclosure. Those to whom essential self-disclosure is granted neither conceive nor witness that kind of separation, except when they consider their knowledge of how the veiled conceive it. Their true distinction follows what I have indicated: the Essence is in no respect other than its essential names, although the names differ among themselves and cannot be separated from the Essence. And the degrees of the keys of the unseen are unequal, some following others; the same has been shown of the derivative divine names, such as Creator, Originator and Fashioner. Remember.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The earlier account treated each rank as a relative terminus; this passage shows that the ranks also have an order in which one proceeds from another, following the corresponding order of the names. The presence of divinity is *wāḥidiyya*, with the four principal names just mentioned. These four are called universal because the Hearing and Seeing are comprehended under the Knowing, while the Speaking is referred to the Powerful and the Willing. Divinity in that respect is the shadow of the Essence in its *aḥadiyya*, in which the seven essential names are gathered as the keys of the unseen.

Yet if *aḥadiyya* contains the same essential names as *wāḥidiyya*, why are they two ranks? The difference is precise and is understood according to the mode in which names are distinctly conceived and actually manifest. In the presence of divinity the Essence can be conceived as distinct from the principal names that appear there; in unicity one does not conceive the Essence and its intrinsic names as genuinely separated. [Continued p. 176.]

title: Self-disclosure, distinction, and ordered names
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** In the rank of divinity the names are manifested in actual differentiation; in the rank of unicity they are not conceived as different from the Essence, because their distinguishing appearances are still gathered in it without being separated. Those veiled from this truth speak as though there were no names and attributes at all at the level of the Essence and as though all names belonged exclusively to the divine presence. Some accordingly deny the possibility of essential self-disclosure: they imagine the Essence as stripped of all attributes and therefore unable to disclose itself, given its independence of the worlds; yet self-disclosure necessarily has the meaning of being manifest.

Those to whom the Essence is disclosed do not conceive the distinction as one between an attribute-less Essence and a presence in which attributes first come to exist. They do not witness such a distinction in essential disclosure. For to disclose itself is to be manifest, and in this perspective the disclosure of the Essence entails the manifestation of all things, since the Real is what appears in everything while also remaining inwardly hidden from all. They can nevertheless understand the distinction when they consider the understanding of those who are veiled. The unveiling of all things includes knowledge of other persons' limited understandings and thus allows them to grasp the distinction **as it appears to those persons**, not as an independent difference in reality.
