What these knowers recognize as a genuine distinction is rather the one already described: at the first rank, the Essence is in no way other than its essential names; at the rank of divinity the names are distinguished from one another in meaning and ruling, while their common reality remains the Essence. They are joined in truth even though the degrees of the names that serve as keys differ. The derivative names are still further ordered. The source text indicates an order of precedence between Knowing, Living, Powerful and Willing, but the exact wording of the first part of that ordering is difficult in the online transcription. In any case the point is **an intelligible order of dependence among divine names**, not a temporal history in which God comes to acquire attributes.

Qūnawī had already drawn attention to the dependence of the derivative names on the principal names in the explanation of the eleventh text. The reader should recall that passage to integrate the ranks, essential names, derivative names and the modes in which each produces its effect. Understand.

title: Text Twenty: The meaning of *munāsaba*, affinity
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī:** If some ranks arise from others, there must be a fitting relationship between what precedes and what follows, such that the subsequent rank is connected with its predecessor.

**Qūnawī:** A chapter on connection.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** That is, on the connection of certain divine names with others, whereby some arise from and are ordered after others.

**Qūnawī:** The secret of affinities (*munāsabāt*) lies in sharing something that removes the rulings of mutual otherness under the aspect in which affinity is established.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The reason that two things can be suitably related is that they share an aspect in virtue of which the differentiation between them is set aside—though in another respect they remain different, so that one can precede the other and the other follow it. Affinity (*munāsaba*) may be **intrinsic** (*dhātiyya*) or a matter of **rank** (*martabiyya*). Intrinsic affinity occurs between the Real and the human being, or between human individuals; rank-based affinity is here treated among human individuals. The two kinds must not be confused.

**Qūnawī:** The first and highest is intrinsic affinity. Between the Real and the human being—who is the intended locus—it is established in two ways. The first concerns the weakness of the effect of the human being as a mirror upon the self-disclosure determined in that mirror, so that it does not give the disclosure a qualification incompatible with divine transcendence, beyond the necessary qualification of determination. That qualification does not impugn the greatness, majesty and oneness of the Real. This also involves freedom from most of the rulings of possibility and from the properties of intervening mediations. The different degrees of the ones brought near and of the solitary perfected ones derive from this aspect.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Intrinsic affinity comes first because it concerns the highest and earliest ranks of manifestation. Among loci it belongs in the fullest sense to the human being, and especially to the perfect human, who is the intended end of manifestation. One aspect of this affinity is negative or privative: the mirror's own fixed reality exerts the least possible limitation on the self-disclosure that appears within it. The less the mirror's individual properties distort the disclosure, the more closely the appearance resembles its source under the aspect of transcendence. Yet a created mirror cannot be altogether without an effect, for what appears in it necessarily has the determination of appearing in *this* mirror rather than another.

Under strict comparison, even that determination is less than the unrestricted Reality. The image is a shadow and cannot equal that whose shadow it is; a determinate shadow cannot encompass the majesty of its source; and determination as distinct from its source implies a relative duality. For these reasons Qūnawī speaks of the **weakness** of the mirror's conditioning action, rather than its complete absence. The difficulty is only resolved when determinate manifestation is not confused with the Essence considered in itself. The same negative affinity comes from the high rank's relative freedom from possible limitations and from intermediary properties. Proximity to the Real means that the rulings of necessity are more evident and the limitations of possibility less evident in the manifestation. [Continued p. 178.]

title: Two aspects of affinity with the Real
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** When the rulings of necessity predominate, intrinsic affinity is established under the first aspect.

**Qūnawī:** The differences in degree of the ones brought near—the poles and solitary individuals—before the Real follow from this aspect.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** One whose mirror has the weaker limiting effect, and whose rank is less burdened by the rulings of possibility, enjoys greater proximity; the contrary condition entails a lesser degree of proximity.

**Qūnawī:** The second aspect of affinity with the Real is according to the servant's share in the form of the divine presence. This share varies with the measure of comprehensive gathering (*jamʿiyya*) in the person. Affinity strengthens or weakens with the narrowness or breadth of the circle of the human being's comprehensiveness, in accordance with the receptivity of that person: one has fewer shares where that circle is restricted, and more where it is expanded.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The second aspect is affirmative: the servant's acquiring the moral qualities and displaying attributes that reflect the divine names, in a way appropriate to created existence. It does **not** mean that a divine attribute migrates from God to the servant, or that numerically the same attribute inheres in two subjects. Rather, the servant receives a share in a spiritual and intelligible *image* of the divine presence, not a material image and not an independent share in the divine Essence. The broader the servant's comprehension of the moral qualities and attributes through which divine names are manifested, the stronger the affinity. The breadth or narrowness of that gathering follows the person's fixed entity as a mirror, its aptitude and receptivity. Consequently the same disclosure is received in unequal degrees.

**Qūnawī:** One who comprehends the attributes and rulings included in necessity and possibility, insofar as they can actually be manifested in any age, and who also possesses affinity under the first aspect, is the one who has perfection. That person is loved by the Real and is intended for his own sake. In virtue of his reality as the **isthmus of isthmuses** (*barzakh al-barāzikh*), he mirrors both the Essence and divinity together with their concomitants. One possessing the first aspect alone is beloved and brought near, but is not the intended end in that same complete sense.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The two aspects are not mutually exclusive; they can coexist. Completeness requires joining the divine attributes understood under necessity with the conditions of the possible ranks, in the full range that may properly appear in each historical age. The qualification about what can appear at a given time is important: not every perfection can be manifested at every age. Its non-manifestation where impossible should not be counted as an intrinsic defect. The commentator connects such completion with prophecy in the age in which it is available, and with the spiritual poles and solitary realized persons after that age. [Continued p. 179.]

title: The perfect human as isthmus of isthmuses
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** The perfected individual exhibits the first affinity, because the mirror's conditioning action is slight and the limitations of possibility are diminished. He also gathers the second affinity, because the possible manifestations of divine attributes and of the cosmic ranks are comprehended in him. He is therefore not simply a favoured creature: his completeness makes him the intended locus in which the two orders are gathered.

He is called the *isthmus of isthmuses* because he joins, in a higher and more inclusive way, what less comprehensive intermediary ranks join only under limited aspects. Other isthmuses mediate necessity and possibility or spirits and bodies. The complete human reality, however, is a mirror of the Essence insofar as it comprehends the intrinsic names without otherness and a mirror of the divine presence insofar as it comprehends the names and their consequences among necessity and possibility. Hence the perfected human possesses the most encompassing created knowledge of the Real through the disclosure of these aspects in him.

The end of creation, in this account, is the manifestation of this comprehensiveness, joining synthesis and detail. The person who possesses only the first mode may be beloved because of purity and proximity and may resemble the divine in having fewer possible limitations; nevertheless, without gathering the relevant whole, he does not have the fully intended comprehensive station. The earlier discussion, especially Text Ten, should be recalled here.

**Qūnawī:** Intrinsic affinity among human beings is likewise established in two ways, corresponding to those two divine–human aspects. One is through a shared temperament (*mizāj*): the two persons' temperaments may lie at the same degree among the degrees of equilibrium covered by the broad range of human temperaments, or their degrees may adjoin one another. This is a great principle in the path of realization, known by immediate experience to very few. For the determinations of human spirits from the spiritual worlds and their unequal nobility and spiritual dignity are connected with the number and strength of the mediations between them and the first principle, and with the multiplicity or weakness of possible limitations. After God's decree and determination, the decisive condition in this ordering is temperament, in accordance with which a spirit becomes individually determined. The temperament closer to genuine equilibrium, the centre around which the perfected souls are determined ... [continued p. 180].

title: Temperament as a condition of spiritual manifestation
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Qūnawī (continuing):** ...receives a more noble and elevated spirit in relation to the ranks of the higher intellects and souls. A temperament further from the point of equilibrium receives what corresponds to a lower rank and a lesser measure of nobility.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Intrinsic affinity between human beings has two aspects analogous to the divine–human case. The first is a relative absence of dissimilarity in the constitution: the two persons may occupy one degree among the different degrees of balance proper to the human species, or neighbouring degrees with no intermediate degree between them. Each class of generated things—mineral, vegetable, animal and human—has its distinctive constitution; each species within a class, each subgroup, and each individual also has its proper constitution. If the constitution required for a species disappears, that kind of individual cannot persist. The species-wide temperament thus comprehends a range of variations in individual and subgroup temperaments, and similarity or adjacency within this range establishes the relevant affinity.

This affinity has special significance, says the commentator, for the relation of spiritual pupils to masters, for their capacity to benefit one another, and for the attraction of one to another. The connection is not commonly understood even experientially among guides. For human spirits become individually determined from spiritual ranks—the intellects and souls—and are differentiated in nobility according to the greater or lesser interposition of other ranks. Fewer and weaker intermediaries mean that the rulings of possibility are less numerous and more attenuated. More powerful or more numerous mediations mean stronger and more numerous limitations. After God's decree, the mixture's degree of equilibrium conditions the manner in which a spirit is determined and manifested in the embodied person.

A temperament in which the opposed elemental tendencies are more completely harmonized approximates unity, and is therefore suited to receiving a nobler spirit. The closest approach to true equilibrium is described as the centre of the circle within which perfect souls are determined, a point at which the elemental tendencies are brought into complete balance. Al-Mahāʾimī marks this as differing from some philosophers' account of equilibrium. The spirit is received according to that degree of suitability, whether it derives, in the cosmology assumed here, from the intellects or from the higher souls. A temperament further removed from the centre corresponds to a lower degree of spiritual manifestation. [Continued p. 181.]

title: From temperamental affinity to spiritual affinity
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** The further the constitution is from genuine equilibrium, the lower the rank of the spirit it is apt to manifest, according to the gradations presupposed by this cosmology.

**Qūnawī:** Know and understand what I have said about a shared temperament, and by understanding it ascend to knowledge of the affinity proper to spirits under the other aspect, the one analogous to the hidden and purely divine intrinsic affinity.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The second human affinity, the one corresponding to the affirmative affinity between human and Real, consists in sharing spiritual qualities, elevations of station, and degrees of realization. This too is related to temperament under the model just described, for a spirit connected with a higher source is more encompassing of the descriptions of necessity, while one bound to a lower determination bears more of the rulings of possibility. Where the two forms of affinity are joined, the individuals share in more complete humanity. Understand.

**Qūnawī:** If you know this through witnessing or through a realized understanding, you will perceive that some spirits have their first station of determination at the Preserved Tablet, others in the spirituality of the Throne from the station of Isrāfīl, others at the Footstool from the station of Mīkāʾīl, and others at the Lote Tree from the station of Jibrīl; and thus in a descending order to the lowest heaven, associated with Ismāʿīl, chief of its angels—peace be upon them all. Then you will recognize that the principal condition of the different ranks of human spirits, after God's prior knowledge, providence, decree and will, is what has just been described concerning temperaments, their closeness to or distance from the point of genuine equilibrium. The divine providence and will are displayed through the sound formation of the bodily constitution, which is followed by the breathing of spirit and its becoming determined. Understand and remember.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The text connects the spiritual ranks with an ordered account of cosmic spiritual principles. The first station of some spirits is the Preserved Tablet, considered in the degree to which their determination becomes perfected through equilibrium. The commentator explains the Tablet as the universal soul, related in one respect to primordial nature and in another to the First Intellect. As an intelligible principle of the balance of constitution it is compared to the heart of the whole world. For that reason Qūnawī does not attach this first case to the spirit presiding over a particular sphere. [Continued p. 182.]

title: The spiritual orders and the breathing of spirit
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** Other spirits are associated with the spirituality of the Throne, including the orders of angels connected with the station of Isrāfīl; other ranks are related to the Lote Tree and Jibrīl, to the heaven of the fixed stars and Riḍwān, to Saturn and its spiritual orders, to Jupiter, Mars, the Sun, Venus, Mercury, and finally the Moon and the lowest heaven. The text records a traditional cosmological hierarchy in which angelic names are assigned to these spheres; the commentator refers the detailed designation of their orders to Ibn ʿArabī's *ʿUqlat al-mustawfiz*. This is an exposition of the hierarchical imagery of the text, not a demonstration of astronomy.

The principal condition of an individual's spiritual place within this hierarchy is, in the model set out, the degree of the embodied constitution's equilibrium, though the author also acknowledges other secondary conditions, including celestial cycles, places and parental circumstances. Above those conditions stands prior divine knowledge and providence, together with decree and will. The effects of providence appear in the proportionate formation of the bodily constitution. That divine fashioning is followed by the breathing of spirit, by which the spirit becomes determined in an outward manifestation rather than remaining under the aspect of its hidden origin. Hence Qūnawī's injunctions to **understand** and **remember**: knowing the ordered spiritual types should lead the reader back to affinity among persons, including their sharing in spiritual characteristics and stations.

**Qūnawī (beginning of the next distinction):** Rank-based affinity, by contrast, is not of one kind only but has a number of aspects. One concerns the original sources from which the determinations of spirits begin, as mentioned above ... [continues p. 183].

title: The original spiritual sources of rank-based affinity
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Qūnawī (continuing):** ...the original sources from which spirits are determined. The source of the highest of them, that is, the spirits of the perfected, is the Mother of the Book (*umm al-kitāb*). The first determination of certain others, in knowledge and in an existence comprehended under unity, is the reality of the Supreme Pen, called the First Intellect and Universal Spirit. Some are determined from the Preserved Tablet, others from the spirituality of the Throne associated with Isrāfīl, some from the spirituality of the Footstool associated with Mīkāʾīl, and others from the rank of Jibrīl at the Lote Tree. This ordering continues down through the types of these spiritual principles to the lowest heaven, whose spiritual chief Ismāʿīl corresponds to what the Peripatetic philosophers call the Active Intellect.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** In treating rank-based affinities, Qūnawī chooses three of their many possible aspects: the source from which the ranks begin, their mode or locus of appearance, and the intermediate stage connecting those beginnings with their manifestations. The first aspect therefore concerns the original *mines* or sources of spirits, not their subsequent perfection. He had previously distinguished the beginning of a spirit's determination from the station at which it becomes complete.

The perfected human spirits—those of prophets, poles and solitary realized individuals—begin from the Mother of the Book, explained here as divine knowledge in its comprehensive rather than differentiated consideration. It is the origin of origins in relation to the intellect and soul, themselves called divine books in the language of this cosmology. The *book* can also signify the great cosmos, whose intelligible principle is knowledge. The beings determined through the Supreme Pen or First Intellect receive a more unfolded mode of determination, one actually distinguished from what is below it while still united by comparison with subordinate ranks. The Pen is so called because of the image of writing and inscription; it is Intellect as comprehending things intelligibly and Universal Spirit as a principle to which lesser spiritual determinations are related.

Other spirits belong to the Tablet, to the Throne and its spiritual orders, to the Footstool, to the Lote Tree, and to further angelic and celestial ranks. Qūnawī's invocation of the Active Intellect at the lowest heaven is intended to bring the hierarchical account into comparison with the philosophers. Al-Mahāʾimī disputes the view that the Active Intellect's action is simply confined to the elemental world. The references to the Peripatetics here belong to a medieval reconstruction of philosophical lineage and cosmology, not to an independently established history of Aristotle and Plato. [Continued p. 184.]

title: The absolute imaginal world as a locus of spirits
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Qūnawī:** Another aspect of affinity is through the spirits' imaginal loci of manifestation. Spirits, despite their unequal ranks, are never without the loci through which they become determined and appear, according to all the realized knowers. The first rank in which human spirits appear, apart from the perfected, is the **absolute imaginal world** (*ʿālam al-mithāl al-muṭlaq*).

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** This is the second aspect among the selected kinds of rank-based affinity. It concerns the starting-point of outward appearance, rather than the original spiritual source considered in itself. The absolute imaginal world is the realm in which spirits may appear through perceptible forms without gross bodies and without requiring the particular faculty of imagination lodged in an individual person's brain. Such forms make distinct appearances possible without reducing the spirit to elemental matter.

The commentator offers a philosophical argument: spirits, considered without any manifesting loci, are simple realities. If they were all of one specific kind without a way of acquiring determinate forms, their differences would not be enough to distinguish individuals as individuals. Merely appealing to different ranks would not fully resolve the problem, because a rank is a general condition rather than the particular determination of an individual. Individual characteristics do not become actual externally before manifestation. The imaginal loci provide the level at which distinct appearances become intelligible and visible. Apart from the perfected human spirits, which are treated as having a higher mode of determination, human spirits first acquire such manifestations in the absolute imaginal world. The commentator refers to Ibn ʿArabī's *ʿUqlat al-mustawfiz* for a corresponding cosmographical account.

**Qūnawī:** Imaginal forms may take their originating material from the subtleties of the powers of this natural life and from its purified and refined substances clothed in the qualities of spirits. Yet their descriptions and states in Paradise are manifested according to their spiritualities and powers and according to the properties of their imaginal loci.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** This indicates that the imaginal world both supplies and receives the loci through which the spirits of the people of Paradise appear. The natural human faculties involved are the animal powers, including outer and inner senses, and the vegetative faculties, as these are refined by righteous acts and noble character. The heart and the soul likewise contribute their refined subtleties, insofar as the heart is purified of domination by the commanding lower soul and the soul is refined in its traits. [Continued p. 185.]

title: Imaginal forms and the degrees of Paradise
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** The heart and soul, once purified and made suitable, acquire qualities corresponding to spiritual forms. The forms found in Paradise are related to them; yet the specific qualities and changes of those forms in Paradise are not merely the direct persistence of earthly matter. They manifest according to the powers of the spirits and the properties of their imaginal bodies. Their capacity to change without the generation and corruption that characterize elemental bodies is adduced as evidence that the relevant level is the imaginal realm. In this way the imaginal world is both the place to which the outward forms of spirits are referred and the source from which they become manifest.

**Qūnawī:** The dwellings of the people of Paradise are manifestations of the ranks of their spirits, both in respect of those spirits' standing before the Real and in respect of their first imaginal loci. The Prophet indicated this through subtle allusions, as when he is reported to have said to ʿAlī that his palace in Paradise would be opposite, or alongside, the Prophet's palace, and similarly concerning al-ʿAbbās. He also spoke of the people of faith as recognizing their dwellings in Paradise more readily than they recognize their homes in this world. This is a consequence of affinity.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The dwellings themselves therefore participate in the imaginal differentiation of the inhabitants: the purer or more attenuated the imaginal locus, the more appropriate its dwelling, without requiring the outward position of the dwelling to correspond identically to its occupant's spiritual station. The distinction matters in the report about ʿAlī's palace being opposite the Prophet's. The Prophet's spiritual rank exceeds that of even the highest saints. Mere physical or imaginal adjacency does not imply equality or near equality of spiritual station. The comparable statement about al-ʿAbbās makes this even clearer. Proximity in the configuration of a dwelling is one kind of relation, proximity in spiritual rank another. Qūnawī calls the reports subtle indications for precisely this reason.

*Source-critical flag:* The online edition includes editorial footnotes saying the editor was unable to locate the particular palace reports about ʿAlī. They are transmitted here as **attributions in the medieval text**, not verified Prophetic sayings. The alternative wording about an adjacent palace should not be reproduced in a definitive edition as an established ḥadīth without an independent isnād search. [Discussion continues p. 186.]

title: The imaginal 'market' and multiple layers of manifestation
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** The report about faithful people finding their dwellings makes the distinction between spiritual rank and imaginal location clearer. He therefore returns to the general principle that all of these are rulings of appropriate relation or affinity.

**Qūnawī:** As for the market of Paradise, in which beautiful human forms are offered and the inhabitants of Paradise may assume whichever of them they desire, it proceeds from a particular channel of the absolute imaginal world, the source and spring of manifestations. Through this channel help flows from the imaginal world to the loci through which the spirits of the people of Paradise appear.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** This answers a possible objection. The original imaginal form was said to arise through the refined faculties and character acquired during earthly life, together with the spirit's powers and the properties of its first imaginal locus. Those characteristics would have been settled at the person's death and resurrection; how, then, can the person adopt new appearances at will in the market? And how can a common market have a meaning beyond the specific dwellings already corresponding to individuals' degrees?

The earlier account concerned **principal forms** and **principal dwellings**. The additional forms, spaces and appearances may proceed as secondary manifestations from particular channels of the inexhaustible absolute imaginal world. Its unrestricted totality is like a great sea, whereas the subsidiary channels provide individualized streams of manifestation. The distinctions of principal rank need not be mirrored by identical distinctions in every subsidiary dwelling. Similarly, the settled properties of the first form need not exhaust the additional qualities that may become manifest through secondary forms. The notion of a channel is introduced to explain continuing supplies of manifestation suitable to distinct subjects. [Continued p. 187.]

title: The nourishment and attire of Paradise
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** The supply of manifestation must continually reach the inhabitants because existence is ever renewed: at every moment there is a new creation. This aid does not arise from the undifferentiated sea under consideration of its absoluteness, since that consideration does not pick out this individual rather than another. Particular channels of imaginal supply explain how one recipient receives one form and another recipient another. The principal forms are called principal because they gather numerous qualities and correspond to numerous channels, while the secondary forms express further and changing qualifications. Understand.

**Qūnawī:** The source of their food, drink, garments and everything in which they delight lies in the grounds of the ranks of their acts, beliefs, dispositions, attributes and degrees of equilibrium in all these matters.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Whatever reaches the inhabitants successively must come through an appropriate particular channel; otherwise there would be an undifferentiated and unvarying supply. Instead they receive continual increase and variety. The rapid return or replacement of forms, such as the restoration of birds and fruits after consumption in descriptions of Paradise, is taken as a sign that their mode of existence is imaginal rather than elemental. The construction of Qūnawī's sentence can also be read so that the 'grounds of the ranks of their works' are the source of their food and clothing. On that reading those enjoyments are themselves determinate forms of the imaginal world; in either case the relative equilibrium of deeds, beliefs, characteristics and other qualities conditions what appears. Understand.

**Qūnawī:** As for the robes and gifts that angels bring from the Real to the generality of the people of Paradise when conveying them to the mound of vision for a visit and audience with the Real, these are manifestations of the rulings of the names and attributes to which those visitors are truly related, whether or not they know it. Through those gifts their affinity with the Real is strengthened, and the subtle bonds of their attachment to Him are enlivened, by means of the names and attributes that exercise a particular lordship over the visitors.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The gifts indicate a further order beyond the forms arising from the imaginal world. The commentator distinguishes the general inhabitants of Paradise, who need particular aids to enter this audience, from the perfected, whose mode of witnessing is not restricted to such periodic visitation. Those who lack the appropriate spiritual realization do not necessarily reach the station of vision. [Continued p. 188.]

title: The gifts brought before the vision of the Real
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** The robes and gifts are described as coming 'from the Real' precisely to distinguish them from the forms generated under the ordinary imaginal channels. They are signs of the rulings of particular divine names and attributes from which the visitors already receive their spiritual order, even if those visitors have not yet recognized this dependence.

The people brought to the mound of vision need a renewed suitability (*istiʿdād*). If a standing suitability alone sufficed for continued vision, there would be no need for a new gift or periodic entrance. Such vision requires an affinity proper to the divine Essence and its names. The direct intrinsic affinity is not acquired by the servant as an autonomous property; it is mediated through the divine names and attributes that possess a particular lordship in relation to each servant. The gifts awaken or renew the delicate ties (*raqāʾiq*) binding them to those names, thereby strengthening the relation that permits their entrance to the station of visitation.

**Qūnawī:** The divine command to the angels at the conclusion of the inhabitants' assemblies of visitation, 'Return them to their palaces,' indicates that the rulings of the affinities supplied by these gifts and robes have reached their limit. The names and attributes which, under their particular operation, established an affinity of proximity and gathering have completed their rule. When the sovereignty of other names and attributes, opposed to those which occasion gathering, becomes manifest, the rulings that distinguish and separate prevail; consequently distance and veiling occur. Understand.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The command to return the visitors demonstrates that the special affinity occasioned by the gifts depends on the operative rulings of names and attributes. If it were a permanent condition independent of those rulings, the vision would not come to an end. The termination of the visitation indicates the termination of the particular conjunction that made it possible. This is not a claim that God changes essentially: what changes is the operative relationship of distinct names to determinate recipients. The following explanation develops their alternation. [Continued p. 189.]

title: The alternation of names and the limits of particular manifestations
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** The relational cause of gathering is the reign of the divine names that bring the visitors near. When their special rulings give way to the complementary rulings of names that establish distinction, the recipients experience separation and a veil from the specific station of vision. They are returned to their dwellings. When the reign of those distinguishing names in turn reaches its end, the names giving rise to gathering again become operative, and the visitors are admitted once more. Every divine name thus has a known scope for its particular rulings and sovereignty, in relation to a place of manifestation and an interval appropriate to that rank. Its lordship is exercised in accordance with those determinate conditions and their order, not as an exclusive power separate from the Essence. This is the sense in which the ruler of a given manifestation changes without any implication of an intrinsically changing divine Essence.

**End of the first online installment of Text Twenty.** The source explicitly marks its continuation. The running text resumes on **printed p. 190** in the next portion of the same web topic. No portion of p. 190 is counted as translated here.

title: Different degrees of the vision and the perfect human
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Qūnawī (passage begins on p. 189 and continues here):** The disparity of the inhabitants' ranks while in the company of the Real depends on their differing stations with respect to Him, the soundness of their convictions concerning God, the correctness of their sciences and spiritual unveilings, and the degree to which they preferred the divine presence to all else in the life that preceded the visitation. The greater or lesser duration of their company, their different degrees of honour in what is addressed to them, and what they understand of that address correspond to these conditions. They also depend on the degree of their presence with Him in accordance with the knowledge or conception they formed, the affinity established by their beliefs, and the particular disclosure granted to each at the station of vision. Know this.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The previous discussion concerned the suitability conferred by the rulings of the divine names and attributes. Qūnawī now returns to intrinsic affinity. Although the visitors all possess a measure of suitability, their degrees of nearness are not equal. The first intrinsic measure concerns how little their particular rank restricts the disclosure. The other concerns their share in comprehensive knowledge and manifestation of the divine presence. Correct beliefs can reinforce these affinities until the servant passes beyond self-regard in extinction toward the Real and subsistence through Him. False beliefs instead restrict apprehension and contribute to veiling. Likewise, preferring God to other things in the life before the vision strengthens love and makes the servant receptive of a fuller manifestation of eternal love.

The length of their audience and the honour they receive in address depend not only on these intrinsic capacities but also on the degree to which they were present to God in the world, their active recollection of Him according to their convictions, and the specific divine names governing the station to which they were brought. Even when they hear one address, the degree to which they comprehend it varies with their stations.

**Qūnawī:** The state of the perfected—may God benefit us through them in this and other things—is different. They have passed beyond the presences of the names and attributes and the disclosures specific to them, into the expanse of essential self-disclosure. They are the kind of people of Paradise of whom the Prophet is reported to have said that their Lord does not hide Himself from them or become veiled from them. They are not confined within Paradise or any other world or presence. As I have indicated elsewhere, Paradise cannot encompass a perfect human being, nor can any other realm. They may appear in whichever loci they wish but are not confined by those forms, places or times. They are with Him wherever He is, and where 'where' itself has no application: without physical interval, distance, veil, transition to a visit or ending through the ruling of a particular time or name. Understand, strive for this and desire to share in some of their exalted stations, for God is the giver of beneficence.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The perfect human is contrasted with the generality, whose forms, nourishment, robes, imaginal loci and periodic visits remain determined by particular names and appearances. The perfected have passed to the station of essential self-disclosure and therefore are not restricted by a specific manifestation or a time of visitation. Their affinity in this account is the highest intrinsic one. [The explanation continues p. 191.]

title: Transcending the limits of the particular imaginal locus
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** The report about a class of the blessed whose Lord is never hidden from them is invoked to express uninterrupted disclosure. Their freedom from confinement is not a denial that they manifest in forms. It means that no form exhausts their reality: they may appear in a locus without becoming bounded by its particular conditions. Similarly, one can speak of their manifestation in times and places without reducing them to those coordinates. As comprehensive loci of divine self-disclosure, they are not brought to God through a journey from one finite location to another, nor is the disclosure exhausted when a particular divine name passes out of its operative station. Such language belongs to a metaphysical account of realized station, not to ordinary spatial motion.

**Qūnawī:** As for the affinities between human beings from the standpoint of their intermediate or *barzakhī* ranks, a model from which the details can be inferred by one who has not witnessed them is given in the Prophet's report of the Night Journey: he saw Adam in the lowest heaven, with the dark silhouettes of the felicitous among his descendants on his right and those of the wretched on his left. When Adam looked rightward he laughed; when he looked leftward he wept. This indicates the general ranks of the two classes.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Here Qūnawī turns to another respect of rank-based affinity: the intermediate life between death and the general Resurrection. The narrative of Adam in the lowest heaven provides an example, or model, from which the different ranks in the barzakh may be understood by people who have not themselves witnessed their arrangement through unveiling. Adam's position at the point of division is associated with his paternal relation to all descendants. The silhouettes to his right and left symbolize their differing outcomes; joy at the former and sorrow at the latter are expressed by his laughter and tears. The image of the right side indicates the more elevated and honoured direction in this interpretation. The commentator infers that the ranks of the unhappy have their locus below the lowest heaven, and those of the fortunate in higher degrees. [Continued p. 192.]

title: Differentiated barzakh stations
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Qūnawī:** The people of unhappiness are those for whom the doors of heaven are not opened at death, and they too have different levels of unhappiness. Reports are given about some such spirits being gathered at Barhūt and other places. Their ranks begin beneath the inward surface of the lowest heaven, where Adam was seen; the lowest are at the places described. As for the generality of the happy, their intermediate station is the lowest heaven, with different degrees gathered within that rank. The elect among the felicitous have higher stations, as indicated by the account of the Night Journey: after Adam in the first heaven came Jesus in the second, Joseph in the third, Idrīs in the fourth, Aaron in the fifth, Moses in the sixth and Abraham in the seventh. Those spiritually joined to these prophets, and their heirs, share their respective stations in differing degrees. The reports concern what the Prophet witnessed in one of his ascensions; Qūnawī also refers to a claim that Abū Nuʿaym collected accounts of thirty-four ascensions.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Those denied the opening of the heavens are described as lacking a heavenly locus at death. Yet the various reports indicate that there is not one level for all of them. Their highest intermediate level is located figuratively at the inner boundary of the lowest heaven, closer to Adam's rank and to the possibility of mercy, while lesser levels are connected with earthly and lower locations such as Barhūt. The cosmographical divisions here are part of the commentator's attempt to reconcile narratives of differing intermediate stations.

The generality of the blessed in the barzakh are likewise not identical in rank, though gathered under the level of the lowest heaven. The elect are above these, including those associated with the stations displayed in the prophetic narrative of the higher heavens. Al-Mahāʾimī treats these associations as differing manifestations of spiritual rank rather than as exhaustive descriptions of all souls. [Continued p. 193.]

title: The ascension report as an example, not an exhaustive cosmic inventory
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** Degrees of recompense and spiritual station differ even among those gathered under one general rank. Those of special felicity rise higher in the intermediate state. The perfected heirs of the prophets likewise manifest in the higher stations, though they are not confined to those manifestations. On this interpretation, a description of the Prophet seeing certain persons in certain heavens reports one witnessing among possible witnessings, not a fixed numerical account of all the blessed.

**Qūnawī:** How could such a state be restricted to the seven prophets mentioned in the account? Prophets and messengers are numerous, and there are perfected ones among them, such as David, whose vicegerency is expressly affirmed, and other eminent messengers. Where are the barzakh ranks of these prophets to be determined after death? The realm above is the heavenly world, while the lower realm contains the ranks assigned to different kinds of unhappiness. Therefore the stations of the prophets, messengers, their perfected heirs and the elect of the felicitous must have corresponding heavenly manifestations after death and before the final gathering. What was narrated of the seven prophets is an illustrative instance of what was not separately enumerated.

The particular appearance of these seven at those heavenly levels was occasioned by an affinity of attributes, acts or states under that mode of witnessing. It does not exhaust their spiritual identities. Thus Yaḥyā may be seen in one account with Jesus and in another with Aaron, because he shares relevant attributes or circumstances with both. Reflect and, God willing, you will be guided.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The plurality of prophets prevents identifying all intermediate levels with the seven figures appearing in one description of the Night Journey. David, for example, is singled out because the Qurʾān expressly says, 'O David, We have made you a vicegerent upon the earth' (38:26); Adam is likewise described as a vicegerent (2:30). Therefore one cannot conclude that other perfected prophets have no rank because they are not named in this particular report. The argument continues on p. 194.

title: Why the places in the miʿrāj reports should not be made exclusive
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** Only two broadly distinguished levels have been introduced in this schematic cosmography: the higher celestial world and the lower elemental world. The lower is described as the station of varying unhappiness, and the assigned levels of Paradise after the final Resurrection are not the subject currently under discussion. Therefore, in this account, the perfected prophets, their heirs and the elect must have intermediate manifestations related to the higher world; the report of seven prophets does not exclude others from it.

The narrative is understood as a sample of the prophet's visionary experiences. When it identifies figures at particular stations, it reveals a relation suitable to that occurrence, not the only location possible for a spiritual reality. Different narrations may associate Yaḥyā with Jesus in one station and with Aaron in another. Qūnawī explains the difference by the predominance of a shared quality, act or state under the particular disclosure. Such a relation can vary; the essential spiritual reality is not thereby fragmented or made into multiple independent persons.

This is why Qūnawī concludes with the command to reflect: the reader is to understand the role of **affinity of a particular aspect** in organizing a visionary representation, without treating the representation as a literal inventory that exhausts the ranks of all messengers and saints.

**Text Twenty ends** in the online transcription here. The next text is Text Twenty-One, beginning on printed p. 195 (subject to verification of the first pagination marker).

title: The Real is pure existence, not unity opposed to multiplicity
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Qūnawī:** An exceedingly noble text.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The preceding text considered the Real and creation, their ranks and their intrinsic and rank-based affinities. The present text turns to the divine unity that comprehends all without the Real concealing creation or creation concealing the Real. It is noble because this station is above the other stations, and exceedingly so because it is their return and their ultimate end.

**Qūnawī:** Know that the Real is pure existence, in which no differentiation obtains. He is one by a real unity, which is not conceived as standing opposite multiplicity, and whose reality in itself, and whose conception by authentic, realized knowledge, do not depend upon conceiving anything contrary to it. Rather it is established through itself and establishes other things; it is not established by another. When we call it *unity*, our purpose is to declare transcendence and to make the matter understood, not to signify the notion of unity as it is conceived in minds veiled from its reality.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The Real, under the first determination and the form of intrinsic divine knowledge, is pure existence. Qūnawī does not say *mere abstraction* or *bare existence*, for the Reality is not restricted to being manifest instead of hidden, or hidden instead of manifest. In itself it contains no division between two independent components, such as quiddity and existence or unrestricted essence and a set of restricting conditions. Its purity is not a deprivation of perfection.

Existence is one because it is necessary through itself and cannot be multiplied into independently necessary existences. But its unity is not a relative unity contrasted with multiplicity; nothing independently opposed to this unity exists. Were it conceived merely through opposition, our knowledge of it would depend on its opposite, and its own reality would depend on something other than itself. Authentic knowledge, here described as realized through unveiling, does not establish unity as an accident added to the Essence through a syllogistic demonstration. Some theologians, says the commentator, conceive the one merely as the contrary of the many; they accordingly conceive unity as additional to the Essence and try to prove it through arguments. The unitary Reality in question, however, is self-established, and other things are established through it.

An objection suggests itself: if the Essence may be conceived under the descriptions one and many, how can unity be identical with it? Qūnawī's answer is that the term *unity* is used to deny the imagined plurality of independently existing realities and to direct the understanding to pure existence. Unity is concomitant with existence: whatever exists has unity insofar as it exists, even when it contains multiplicity under another consideration. The many are not many simply because each lacks unity; the plurality itself has a unity under which it is gathered. One can distinguish intellectually between the different respects without multiplying the source of being.

The commentator considers an objection that multiplicity, as multiplicity, receives existence but not unity. He replies that the plurality of many things is itself intelligibly gathered through a unity, even if unity is attributed to a collection mediately. A further objection concerning the division of a formerly continuous body is taken up on p. 196.

title: Non-oppositional unity and its inaccessibility to definition
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** Someone may ask: if unity were identical with existence, then physically dividing a thing would amount to annihilating one existence and producing two new existences. Yet piercing a sea with a needle does not annihilate the sea and create two new seas. The reply is that an incidental division need not destroy the substantial unity under which the sea remains one. Even if one grants the production of plurality under one description, the former unity is lost *under that description* rather than proving that pure existence has been annihilated. The analogy is not a proof that the Essence is one thing which can be split into distinct divine existences. The term unity here is not the ordinary numerical unity of one object opposed to two.

**Qūnawī:** Once this is understood, we say that God, in respect of the unity just described, and apart from the loci of manifestation and the descriptions attributed to Him through His appearance in them, is not apprehended, comprehended, known, characterized or described.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Because the Real's pure existence admits no genuine difference within itself and His unity is not one contrasted with many, He cannot be singled out and fully grasped under that consideration. Defining a thing ordinarily depends on distinguishing it from another through shared genus and differentiating difference, or through properties peculiar to it. But a Reality without internal composition, genus or specific difference cannot be defined by the *ḥadd*. Nor can it be adequately grasped through a descriptive *rasm* made from its concomitant properties, since those properties belong to the ranks under which He is manifested and are not additional parts of His Essence considered in itself.

Thus there is no intrinsic predicate that sets Him apart from independent equals, because such equals are not possible; nor any accidental predicate that comprehends Him in Himself. The same holds when one removes from consideration the manifestations and the descriptions that belong to Him only by relation to those manifestations. The denial of comprehensive knowledge does not deny real knowledge under the divine names and effects. It denies that such mediated comprehension should be mistaken for exhaustive knowledge of pure existence as such.

**Qūnawī:** Whatever is apprehended in concrete individuals or witnessed among originated things, whatever the manner in which the human being apprehends it and whichever presence contains the witnessing—setting aside what is apprehended of abstract meanings and realities in their unseen presence through unveiling—when it is apprehended in some locus of manifestation, what is perceived is a diversity of colours, lights and surfaces, differing in quality and quantity, or their likenesses in an imaginal world connected with the human constitution or in an imaginal world in one respect separate from it. The images may correspond to appearances in the external world or to the externally given elements from which they are formed. The multiplicity in all these cases is sensibly grasped; their oneness is understood by intellect or intuitive insight. All are rulings of existence, or forms of the relations of His knowledge, or attributes inseparably attached to it as it appears in association with each individual thing, in and through and for that thing according to its receptivity. Call them by whichever of these descriptions you wish: they are not pure existence itself. [Continued p. 197.]

title: Why what is seen in the world is not pure existence itself
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The evident objection is that Qūnawī first denies perception of pure existence and then speaks of the Reality as present in all individuals and in the abstract realities disclosed by unveiling. Have we not perceived it in the sensible realm, and known it in the hidden realm?

He distinguishes between what is known through abstract meanings and what is witnessed in determinate loci. Abstract intelligibles, in their own degree of being known, are not the externally existent Reality in its purity. The witnessing of concrete things, whether by senses, imagination, heart, spirit or intellect, and whether in a divine or created presence, necessarily encounters some **locus of manifestation**. The senses directly perceive such qualities as colour and light; surfaces with different qualities and quantities are apprehended in conjunction with them. What appears inwardly may be an image in the imagination linked to the human body or in the imaginal realm that, as a rank, is not reducible to that particular bodily faculty. In either case the apprehension is of a qualified appearance, not the pure source of appearance.

The plurality of these appearances can be sensed. The unity that renders them intelligible is grasped by understanding or by a form of intuition; it is not itself another coloured surface. To apprehend the many determinate forms is therefore not the same as directly grasping the unity concomitant with existence in itself. The commentator stresses that different organs and faculties may perceive distinct aspects without thereby receiving pure existence as a sensuous object. [The argument continues p. 198.]

title: Rulings, relational forms and attributes of existence
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** An objector says: if the unity in concrete things can be understood or intuited, then surely existence itself is apprehended. The reply is that the question concerns **complete apprehension**. The unity abstracted from a determinate object does not amount to the absolute unity of existence, which cannot be contained by that limited object. What the witness sees is the rulings and effects of existence as it is related to the individual realities to which existence is ascribed.

This relation must not be imagined as physical contact between two self-subsisting objects. It is the mystery of the Real's appearing **in** the realities of the things, **through** them in their determinate manifestations, and **for** each of them in accordance with its capacity. Under one description what is encountered is the ruling of existence in connection with the entities; under another it is the form of a relation of divine knowledge; under another it is a concomitant attribute of that appearance. These descriptions are not simply interchangeable: an attribute attaches to a subject, a ruling may also be attributed to one of its attributes, and a form occurs not within the unconditioned Essence but in the relevant loci. Yet each describes an aspect of what is manifested, not the pure existence of the Real as such.

**Qūnawī:** For existence is one, and what is one cannot be apprehended by something other than itself precisely under the respect in which the other is different from it. The one, insofar as it is one, is not apprehended by the many insofar as they are many, nor conversely. Human apprehension does not take place through a unity identical with the real unity of existence, but through the human being's being a reality qualified by existence and life, having knowledge established in it, possessing an affinity with what it seeks to know, and being free of impediments to knowledge. It therefore apprehends through its multiplicity, not through pure unicity; so the Real considered without any multiplicity cannot be grasped in this way. There are secrets of the soul concerning this matter, discussed at greater length in Qūnawī's *Kashf satr al-ghayra ʿan sirr al-ḥayra*, and the work will clarify it further.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** What is encountered under determinate appearances is not pure existence, for the latter is one, whereas the faculties that ordinarily apprehend are multiple in respect of their conditions. A relation of complete otherness would prevent perfect identification with that which is known. The more detailed epistemological argument proceeds on p. 199.

title: The composite conditions of human apprehension
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** The many cannot fully apprehend the One under the aspect of multiplicity, for the many under that aspect possess distinct determinations. Conversely, the One considered in pure unity cannot contain a plurality of independently inscribed impressions under that very respect. Qūnawī therefore qualifies the denial carefully: the Real is not known *by another insofar as that other differs from Him*. The same human reality may be considered under a different aspect, but ordinary human knowing does not proceed from the absolute unity of existence.

The human knower must exist; must be living; must possess the faculty or presence of knowledge; must have an appropriate affinity with the object; and must be free of obstacles that prevent apprehension. Under such conditions the human being is a composite of determinate considerations. Even the description 'human being' implies a reality that has existence and the qualifications by which it is known. The person consequently knows what can be known under the relations of the names and manifestations, rather than knowing unconditioned Being by an act attributable simply to the knower's ordinary humanity.

Does this deny the essential self-disclosure mentioned previously for the perfected? The commentator says no. Such disclosure is not given while the knower's ordinary self-regard remains the dominating principle. The egoity of the witness is overwhelmed by the light of unitary disclosure. To the degree that real unity prevails in the witness, apprehension is no longer attributed to the human being *as a many-conditioned human being*. This is a shift in the **aspect of the act of knowing**, not evidence that a finite faculty has captured pure existence within its own delimitation.

**Qūnawī:** Let us return to the matter at hand. In respect of the Real, existence is the very Essence; in whatever is other than Him it is additional to the thing's reality. The reality of each existent consists in the relation of its eternal determination in its Lord's knowledge. The realized among the people of God call it a *fixed entity* (*ʿayn thābita*); others call it a *quiddity* (*māhiyya*), 'the known non-existent,' 'the established thing,' and similar expressions.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The discussion now returns from the epistemological digression to the crucial contrast between divine pure existence and the quiddities of contingent beings. The divine Essence does not first subsist as a quiddity and then receive existence as a property superadded to it. A contingent reality, by contrast, can be distinguished from the existence manifested through it. The argument is examined in terms familiar from philosophy and kalām on p. 200.

title: Why God's existence is not additional to His Essence
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Suppose the necessary Real had a quiddity distinct from the existence that actualizes it. His existence would then depend upon the quiddity as a support or determining ground. What depends on something other than itself is possible rather than necessary in itself. If a quiddity were said to give existence to itself, the thing that confers existence would need to be prior to what receives it. In respect of giving existence, the supposed quiddity must itself already exist, leading to priority of a thing over itself or an infinite regress. God therefore cannot possess a quiddity that first exists independently and subsequently becomes actual by an added existence.

An opponent objects that causal or constitutive priority need not always be priority in actual existence. Possible quiddities may be conceived as capable of receiving existence, while the constituents of a composite definition are prior to the whole even though they are not separately actual entities. The commentator distinguishes the cases. The **giver** of existence must be understood as actually able to give it; the **recipient** of existence may be conceived as lacking that act; a **constitutive part** of a quiddity is considered without affirming or denying its actual existence. These are three different modes of priority, and the comparison does not establish that a necessary existence could receive being from its own non-existent essence.

If it is said that a thing could confer existence on itself without previously existing, otherwise it would have to exist twice, the answer is that the supposed existent source would then be different from the quiddity it actualizes. One would have to posit an existence before the existence allegedly received, which simply renews the difficulty. The commentator further disputes the claim that constitutive parts have no actual or intelligible priority at all.

The other part of Qūnawī's thesis is that, for contingents, existence is **additional to quiddity**. The commentator offers several considerations. First, the possible quiddity, considered as such, admits non-existence, whereas a quiddity conceived as identical with existence would not admit non-existence in that same respect. An objector replies that 'admitting non-existence' need not mean a quiddity positively subsists without being; it may mean simply that the existent thing can cease to exist. The commentator insists that the fixed reality is not a newly produced entity in divine knowledge and that pure existence, insofar as existence, is not annihilated by the disappearance of one of its determinate loci. Second, a quiddity can be conceived while its existence is doubted: the concept and its extra-mental realization are therefore distinct. The detailed rejoinder is continued on p. 201.

title: A contingent quiddity is not its existence
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing the discussion begun p. 200):** The opponent had maintained that one doubts external existence, not the mental existence that consists in apprehending a quiddity. Yet the existence and nature of mental existence are themselves disputed, and the fact that a concept is apprehended does not by itself establish the existence of an extra-mental object corresponding to it. Moreover, before a quiddity is conceived mentally it need not have the particular mental existence it later acquires. Thus one must distinguish its quiddity from that mode of mental presence, just as one distinguishes it from external actuality. Since it differs from each of these specific existences, the commentator concludes that quiddity and existence taken in general are not simply identical.

He notes that these issues have been discussed more extensively in the introduction; further technical questions belong to works of kalām and philosophy rather than to the immediate purpose of this Sufi commentary.

Qūnawī identifies the specific reality of each thing—the reality to which existence is related—as **the relation by which it is eternally determined in the knowledge of its Lord**. The eternal Essence contains many intrinsic modalities (*shuʾūn*) without their being distinguished from one another at that first rank. Divine knowledge bears a relation to each modality; through that relation it is determined as an intelligible form in eternal knowledge. Through the connection of existence with that form the corresponding thing is manifest as an actual existent.

Hence theologians say that each thing has a reality by which it is what it is and differs from other things, whether by inseparable or separable characteristics. It is the answer to 'What is it?'—for example, 'rational animal' when one asks what a human being is. The phrase **relation of its determination** excludes the undifferentiated modalities and pure existence, which considered in itself has no such relation. The phrase **in the knowledge of the Real** excludes the quiddity as it appears in the world through manifested existence, and distinguishes divine knowledge from creatures' merely abstract ways of conceiving a quiddity. The word **eternally** excludes the object's being known under the respect of its actual external existence, which is an additional determination, not the quiddity considered in itself.

Among the realized people of God this eternal, intelligibly determined reality is called a **fixed entity** (*ʿayn thābita*): an entity because of its determinate intelligibility, fixed because of its establishment in divine knowledge, without thereby possessing external existence. Others call the relevant object a *quiddity*. Some theologians who distinguish existence from quiddity speak of the *known non-existent*, while certain Muʿtazilites affirm the possible non-existent as a *fixed thing*. These labels belong to different conceptual frameworks, not a claim that all those schools agree in doctrine. Among the people of God, 'thing' may be reserved in a particular usage for something that is existent, and the Qurʾānic phrase 'I created you before, when you were nothing' (19:9) is invoked to clarify that usage. [Terminological discussion continues p. 202.]

title: From the One only one: the common effusion of existence
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī (concluding the terminology):** These disagreements over *thing*, *non-existent* and quiddity open on longer debates, but the present purpose does not require pursuing them all.

**Qūnawī:** The Real, considered in respect of the unity of His existence, gives rise to only one, since it is impossible for the One, as One, to manifest or produce what is more than one. But that one, in our view, is **general existence** (*al-wujūd al-ʿāmm*), effused upon the fixed entities of the generated things, those already manifest and those whose manifestation is known in advance though it has not yet appeared. This existence is common to the Supreme Pen—the first existent also called the First Intellect—and all other existents, as has been mentioned by philosophical thinkers. For the realized knowers there is, in truth, nothing but the Real and the world; and the world is not something additional to the realities known to God which are qualified by manifested existence.

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Having shown that the Real is existence itself, Qūnawī now derives the implication of its unity. The One taken simply as One cannot immediately have multiple heterogeneous products under that single undivided aspect. The claim concerns both *manifesting* and *bringing into existence*, so it must not be understood as a purely philosophical theory that excludes the Sufi account of disclosure.

The commentator introduces a formulation attributed to the philosopher and theologian Naṣīr al-Dīn al-Ṭūsī. The principle was nearly evident in itself, Ṭūsī is said to maintain; opposition largely arose from not understanding the strict meaning of pure unity. If a simple thing is, in itself and without added consideration, that from which effect A must proceed, and also that from which independently different effect B must proceed, the concept of its giving rise to A differs from the concept of its giving rise to B. If these are real and distinct grounds in the cause, the supposedly simple cause contains different determinations and is no longer one from every aspect. To preserve its complete simplicity one must either account for the difference at another level or deny two immediate diverse effects under that same strict aspect.

The immediate single emanation is **not**, in Qūnawī's distinctive construction, the First Intellect taken as one created intermediary through which God must subsequently cause everything else. It is the universal effusion of existence itself, common to the First Intellect and the rest of the world. That distinction becomes central to the lengthy debate that follows.

title: Al-Ṭūsī's principle and objections to it
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The presentation of al-Ṭūsī's argument continues. If the two effects are said to be concomitants of one simple principle, the distinction of the aspects grounding their necessary production returns. If one is made constitutive and the other consequential, the consequent either proceeds from an aspect identical with the constituent, making its distinct production unexplained, or it proceeds from a distinct grounding aspect, implying composition in the cause. If the differences are placed among constituents of the cause, the supposed cause ceases to be simple; if they are made independent consequences, the original explanatory difficulty recurs.

The resulting diversity may concern material composition, as in a body composed of form and matter; the multiplication of what a thing possesses after it is constituted, as in an intellect whose quiddity and existence are distinguishable; or a division into parts and individual instances. In each case a relevant multiplicity is introduced somewhere. The commentator reports this as al-Ṭūsī's formulation before turning to objections.

A critical question is pressed: would not the reasoning also prohibit a simple cause from producing **even one** effect?
