We can conceive the simple Essence and still ask whether it causes a particular effect. The concept of being this cause is therefore distinct from the concept of the Essence. If the causal aspect is constitutive, the principle appears composite; if it is a concomitant, a regress seems to arise until a constitutive aspect is reached. Such a problem would concern the difference between the Essence and its causal description, not specifically the existence of two effects. The commentator replies that the single intrinsic causal respect can be nothing other than the Essence itself, without adding another real constituent, whereas **two genuinely distinct intrinsic causal grounds** cannot both be identical with that very simple Essence under the same strict respect.

Another objection rejects the regress on the ground that a causal aspect may be merely conceptual. The response distinguishes a mere verbal or mental consideration from a real ground of efficacy. If a thing is genuinely an agent of an effect, there must be a sufficient explanatory respect in virtue of which that effect follows; otherwise any thing would be capable of producing any other thing. The discussion continues with the objection that one would be positing both the causal principle and its causal efficacy as two original things.

title: Al-Rāzī's objections and the two meanings of 'proceeding'
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The response to the foregoing objection is that the First Principle is a cause through its very reality; were an additional independent cause of its efficacy required, that additional factor would itself be the primary explanation, contrary to the hypothesis of the First Principle.

Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī is then cited as objecting that a single thing can bear many negations, many predicates and many receptivities. One thing can be neither stone nor tree, a human can be described by different postures, and a substance can receive diverse accidents such as colour and motion. If every difference of predicate or relation required a multiplicity in the source, it would absurdly follow that a simple thing could be described, negated or affected under only one respect.

Al-Ṭūsī's reply, as reported by the commentator, is that these are not cases of many independent effects proceeding immediately from the single thing considered in itself. Negation requires the thing negated as well as the subject from which it is denied; predication presupposes both subject and predicate; receptivity concerns the receiving subject and the different things received. A body receives colour under a condition of being affected and motion under a condition relevant to its change of place. The multiplicity here belongs to the factors or relations required by the cases, not merely to a simple cause producing two immediate diverse beings under exactly one aspect.

To explain the difference, *proceeding* (*ṣudūr*) is distinguished in two senses. First, it can mean the relation of causal dependence between a cause and its effect once both are considered; this relation presupposes the two terms. Second, it can mean the cause's intrinsic being such that a given effect proceeds from it. That respect is explanatory prior to the effect and to the relation subsequently attributed to the two. The argument about the One concerns this **second** sense. If the cause produces one effect purely by what it is, its causal sufficiency may be identical with its Essence. If different effects require two distinct intrinsic grounds, the alleged simple cause is given different respects that need explanation. The objection from multiple external negations or predicates therefore does not straightforwardly refute the principle.

A further objection asks whether the very act of creation implies two products, quiddity and existence. The dialogue continues p. 205.

title: Quiddity, existence and a multiplication of relations
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The first new objection is that causing one thing seems to cause both **what it is** and **that it is**—quiddity and existence—so the One would already produce two. The commentator answers according to the distinction previously defended: the quiddity as eternally known is not a newly made existent in itself; what is given in the world is its manifested existence. If, for the sake of argument, one treats a quiddity as made, one would still have to ask how its being made relates to its becoming existent, and that would not simply furnish two coordinate immediate products.

A geometrical analogy is then considered. A central point is opposite many points on a circle. Being opposite one particular point is a different relation from being opposite another. Must the single central point therefore contain a plurality of different constitutive aspects? No: each relation has **two terms**—the central point and a particular circumference point. The difference arises from distinct relational termini, not from a real multiplicity hidden inside the central point itself. Another objection cites the receptivity of substance to location and to various positive accidents. The reply is that the simplicity of the relevant substance, the precise existential status of the effects, and the distinct enabling conditions must first be established; one cannot assume that two different predicates of receptivity prove two independent creations by a cause that is one in every respect.

A further objection attacks an infinite causal chain: if the One produces one thing, which produces the next, and so on, are not all effects compelled to form a single linear sequence? Experience shows that two individuals need not causally produce one another. Al-Ṭūsī's response, as transmitted here, allows a branching order through **combined conditions**: one effect may issue from the first source; later effects may arise from the source considered together with an earlier effect or other conditions. There need not be a relation of direct cause between every two items. An objector replies that causing the first effect without a condition and the second with an additional condition seem again to be different causal respects in the source; the rejoinder places the new composite explanation in the combined terms rather than in the first source considered alone. [Continued p. 206.]

title: The Akbarī reinterpretation of the first effect
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** The earlier objection can also be resisted by distinguishing the existing effect's received existence from its possible quiddity. An effect can be one *as an existent* while still allowing a variety of further relations and conditions in what follows from it. The treatment of al-Ṭūsī's principle shows why Qūnawī chose the language of both **manifesting** and **bringing forth**: his argument must apply to the Akbarī notion of disclosure as well as to the philosophers' language of production.

But the principle *'from the One, insofar as One, only one'* had provoked substantial criticism from theologians. If the immediate product were necessarily one particular created intelligence and all other things had to proceed through a chain of finite intermediaries, it could seem to deny God's immediate creative efficacy with regard to ordinary events. Some critics condemned the philosophers who drew such a consequence. Qūnawī, however, accepts the aspect of the principle that expresses simplicity while rejecting the conclusion that God's sole immediate product is the First Intellect.

**Qūnawī's point, explained by al-Mahāʾimī:** The one effusion is the **universal and simple existence** (*al-wujūd al-ʿāmm al-muṭlaq al-basīṭ*). Its appearance in many realities does not compromise its true unity, because the multiplicity concerns the determinations and relations of manifestation. Just as the First Intellect may be approached under several relations without being thereby reduced to distinct unrelated existences, the one effusion may be manifested in numerous fixed entities known eternally to God. The distinction between what has appeared, what will appear and what is never to appear follows the eternally known order of possibilities; it does not imply that all possibilities are manifested simultaneously or that divine knowledge comes to acquire new content. All are known according to what they are, and the temporal order of their appearance follows the established order of disclosure.

The Supreme Pen, also named the First Intellect in the relevant philosophical vocabulary, may be called the first **created** locus receiving that common existence. The commentator cites reports of the Pen and Intellect as first created, but these reports require independent verification. In any case the Pen is so called for its role in the image of inscription and the Intellect for its immaterial intelligibility. This first locus does not monopolize God's efficacy. The other things of the world, including continually arising events, are not thereby independent of the Real or dependent on a created intelligence as an *exclusive* necessary creative intermediary.

title: Against a necessary created intermediary between God and the world
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The commentator notes that theologians other than some Muʿtazilites generally reject both the philosophical principle in its rigid derivative interpretation and the necessary intermediary that interpretation seems to impose between God and other existents. Qūnawī's alternative is not merely to replace the intermediary with a different first created thing. He denies the need for that created intermediary by returning to the relation of the Real to knowledge and existence.

If one says that the universe is composed of realities eternally known to God which are then qualified by external manifestation, where could an independent created intermediary be inserted? Between the Real and His own existence there can be none, because His existence is His very Reality. Between the Real and the eternally known quiddities there likewise cannot be an independently existing entity through which their eternal knownness first arises. Nor does treating the world as the joint consideration of existence and its possible determinations establish a separate creator standing in between. The commentary begins articulating these alternatives here and continues them in the next instalment.

**Qūnawī (lemma beginning in the next instalment, translated under p. 207–208 boundary):** The realities of things, insofar as they are objects of knowledge whose forms are eternally determined in the Real's intrinsic knowledge, cannot be *made*: new events cannot occur within the divine Essence, nor can the Real be a receptacle containing something other than Himself or something contained by another. Other consequences also make such a 'making' impossible. Making concerns existence: what has no external existence is not made as an externally subsisting entity. Otherwise eternal knowledge would produce a new effect within itself, and the known forms would have to be co-existent with their Knower as independent beings or the Knower would be a receptacle affected by Himself. All these outcomes violate the purity of His unity. [The source expands the argument on p. 208.]

*Pagination note:* The forum has an internal instalment break here and resumes with the Qūnawī lemma before the printed **208** marker. Accordingly, the lemma spans the printed p. 207–208 transition; it is not a new text-number or a new chapter.

title: Why the fixed entities cannot be made *as eternally known*
speaker_layer: English working rendition (Qūnawī / al-Mahāʾimī voices indicated). Arabic transcription pending import.
editorial_note: The new page has a preliminary English translation, not the Arabic paragraph. Its online Arabic source is linked above. The passage has not been critically established or independently collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The fixed realities are **not made** under the aspect of their being eternally known and differentiated as forms within divine knowledge. They are not two independent kinds of existence alongside the one existence manifested through things. If one were to make the quiddities themselves separate new entities in that eternal knowledge, one would have to say that they were originated; but the knowledge of the Real cannot have newly originated accidents subsisting within it. Knowledge is not other than His Essence in the way a creaturely faculty may be other than its owner, and the necessary eternal divine attribute does not become the locus of acquired and perishable forms.

A distinction of aspects must nonetheless be retained. A form known by **creatures**, or as known under God's outward disclosure through the loci of creation, may be said to be made in relation to that new manifestation. But the same quiddity **as eternally known to God** is not produced by an act that occurs later than His knowing it. It does not follow that created things are self-existent or uncreated in their outward existence; their actuality is the very thing that is bestowed. The immutable known content and the act of its manifestation must be kept apart.

The commentator presses the dilemma. If the fixed entities were made within God's eternal knowledge, would they originate temporally within what has no temporal beginning? An originated event within eternity is contradictory. If they were instead imagined as co-existing with their eternal Knower through independent existence, the account would introduce a plurality of eternal substances. If the Knower received them through an effect of Himself upon Himself, His Essence would be rendered the subject of a new internal affection. If they were treated as other entities contained in Him, or as containing Him, He would become a spatial or ontological receptacle or something receptively contained. Each is denied.

The very notion of making applies to what is actualized: what does not have external existence is not produced as a separately existing entity. The fixed entities have no independent external actuality, though existence appears through and with them and is ascribed to them. To say otherwise would make the divine knowledge, which embraces everything eternally, acquire new realities in order to know them. It would also imply that quiddities already existed independently *before* existence was effused upon them, making the new giving of existence redundant—**the acquisition of what is already obtained** (*taḥṣīl al-ḥāṣil*). The commentator therefore concludes that the pure unity of the Real, the eternal intelligibility of the fixed entities and the real creation of their manifest existence must be affirmed together.

**End of p. 208.** The argument continues on **p. 209** with further examples, followed by the discussion of how one existence is attributed to the possible things in their manifestation. The twenty-first text is **not yet complete**.

title: Why quiddities are not *made* as eternally known
speaker_layer: Qūnawī primary lemmata and al-Mahāʾimī commentary — working English translation
editorial_note: Working first-pass English from online Arabic transcription; source Arabic has not been embedded or critically collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing the argument):** Consider also that certain necessary concomitants attach to quiddities precisely insofar as they are what they are. Four, for example, is even. Were one to posit a four that was not even, it would not be four. It follows that the quiddity must be determinate in consideration independently of the particular individual existences (*huwiyyāt*) through which it might be manifested. Here *huwiyya* refers to existence. If quiddities themselves were produced, what produced them would have to precede existence; but precedence of this sort is impossible. Thus realities, insofar as God knows them, are not made, although it is permissible to speak of their being made under another consideration.

Since they are not made in themselves, two distinct existences do not thereby arise. A plurality of existences would follow if the distinct quiddities possessed existence in their own right, so that existence itself differed essentially with each different quiddity. Rather, considered in itself, existence is one with regard to the Real and the created order. It is shared by the many realities in respect of its appearance in and through them. Its source is the Real, from whom it overflows upon them as sunlight falls upon what faces the sun.

**Qūnawī:** “This single existence, which is ascribed to created possibilities, is not different in its reality from the true, hidden existence abstracted from entities and loci of manifestation, save through relations and considerations—such as appearance, determination, multiplicity acquired through conjunction, receptivity to the rule of sharing, and similar qualifications that attach to it by its connection with loci of manifestation.”

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Qūnawī says “ascribed to created possibilities” because the existence in question does not attach to any other class of beings. The possibilities cannot serve as intermediaries through which existence is first obtained for some of them or through which its relations and considerations first arise. As for existence itself: in reality it is not different from the true hidden existence, considered apart from entities and manifestations. Its being outwardly displayed and connected with manifestations does not generate a second reality of existence. On this account it cannot require a created intermediary. Even were one to concede, for the sake of argument, a distinction from existence which is necessary in itself, the existence in the different possibilities would differ only by relations of attribution, not by different self-subsisting existences. As for the relations and considerations, these arise on account of the loci of manifestation, which as fixed entities are not independently existent. [The discussion continues on p. 210.]

title: No created intermediary between God and the world's existence
speaker_layer: Qūnawī primary lemmata and al-Mahāʾimī commentary — working English translation
editorial_note: Working first-pass English from online Arabic transcription; source Arabic has not been embedded or critically collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī:** If one now considers the loci as actually existent, then the First Intellect would not be the necessary intermediary for everything beneath it. Each locus would be the intermediary for its **own** determination and relational properties, not for existence as such. Appearance in a locus, determination by it, and multiplication according to the number of loci are the principal considerations. The first two arise from existence's conjunction with the loci; the third arises because this conjunction permits participation or sharing. The remaining qualifications likewise attach in consequence of existence's relation to the manifestations.

Thus each manifestation occasions its own relations and attributes; it does not give existence its existence. There is consequently no intermediary between the Real and creation in the sense under dispute. What is thought to be an intermediary is merely the occasion **at which** certain determinations arise, not an independently creative power **by which** they arise. If no such intermediary is needed with respect to the quiddity, existence, relations, or properties of the world, combining these aspects cannot suddenly require one.

There is nonetheless another sense in which mediation must be considered: namely, in the connection between the Real and the contingent realities. Since He is essentially free of need for the worlds, this 'intermediary' cannot be an independently existing item within the world, whether taken as its reality or as its existence; rather, it pertains to the Real and His names and attributes.

**Qūnawī:** “The fountainhead of the loci of existence, considered in respect of its conjunction [with them], is the presence of His self-disclosure, the station of His determination and descent: the *ʿamāʾ* mentioned by the Prophet. It is the station of lordly descent, the wellspring of the essential, all-merciful generosity from the unseen of He-ness and the veil of the majesty of I-ness. Within this *ʿamāʾ* is determined the rank of the first, unseen, eternal conjunction (*nikāḥ*), which opens the presences of the divine names through primordial essential orientations. Before long we shall unseal the key to its keys, God willing.”

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The fountainhead means the basis upon which possible realities become mirrors displaying true existence. This is not a conjunction of two bodies, nor of an accident inhering in a subject, nor a container holding what is contained. It is the manifestation of existence in these realities; the fixed entities become loci through which it is disclosed, after the Real's manifestation to Himself in Himself. Its 'descent' is consequently a descent in rank toward differentiated disclosure, not movement from a higher place to a lower place. The station named *ʿamāʾ* is invoked to explain that rank. [The printed page ends in the midst of the report and its elucidation.]

title: *ʿAmāʾ*, second determination and the first conjunction
speaker_layer: Qūnawī primary lemmata and al-Mahāʾimī commentary — working English translation
editorial_note: Working first-pass English from online Arabic transcription; source Arabic has not been embedded or critically collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The prophetic report under discussion describes God as being in *ʿamāʾ* before creation, with no air above or beneath it [the wording and transmission require independent verification]. The commentator identifies *ʿamāʾ* here with the presence of *wāḥidiyya*—the rank at which distinctions among the names become intelligible. As an image, it is like a thin veil between the created world and the first determination. It is the source of the loci of existence and the 'intermediary' only in this qualified sense: the rank through which the self-disclosure of what is already essentially real is articulated in relation to possible realities.

This is called the lordly descent from the first to the second determination, and the outflow of all-merciful generosity. The name *al-Raḥmān* encompasses the names of divine action by which every recipient is given the existence appropriate to it. In the first determination the affairs and names are not distinguished; pure existence is considered without their differentiation. In the station of lordship and merciful existence their distinctions become manifest. The *ʿamāʾ* is therefore the rank of the first *nikāḥ*: a primordial orientation of love, illustrated by the saying, “I was a hidden treasure and loved to be known” [traditional Sufi citation; it must not be presented as a sound prophetic ḥadīth without verification].

It is called conjunction because by it the Real, who needs no world, is related to the realities capable of manifesting His names. Alternatively, it is called this because it precedes the differentiated manifestation of the names themselves. This rank opens the presences of the **divine** names: names of disclosure are relationships between Essence and manifestations, while the essential names have no such need of external loci, since at that first consideration they are not distinct from the Essence. The divine names become differentiated through the eternal essential orientations toward the divine affairs, bringing into manifest actuality what was comprehended in unity. [The lengthy note on the metaphor of *nikāḥ* in the printed source is an editor's note, not translated as al-Mahāʾimī's own commentary.]

title: The first of two considerations of existence
speaker_layer: Qūnawī primary lemmata and al-Mahāʾimī commentary — working English translation
editorial_note: Working first-pass English from online Arabic transcription; source Arabic has not been embedded or critically collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** The purpose of the first conjunction is to bring into actuality in a locus those possible determinations and qualifications that are contained potentially in existence. Qūnawī's promised key may be the essential loving orientation, or perhaps the inclusion of many considerations and affairs within existence without their prior separation.

**Qūnawī:** “If you have understood, existence admits of two considerations. The first is existence merely as existence, which is the Real. From this aspect, as already indicated, there is no multiplicity, composition, quality, attribute, name, description, relation, or judgment; rather it is sheer existence. And our saying ‘existence’ is for the sake of making the matter understood, not because that is a true name designating Him. His name is identical with His attribute, and His attribute is identical with His Essence.”

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Having spoken of the fountainhead of manifestations and of *ʿamāʾ* as a real rank prior to the created order, Qūnawī distinguishes two considerations of existence. The first is sheer existence in the rank of *aḥadiyya*. Here the Real is necessary in Himself, and none of the distinctions between being and quiddity, or between other constituents, can be admitted as an actual composition. Neither contingent qualities nor essential epithets have a distinct identity at that rank. There is no name over against what it names, no representation of Him, and no relation to another, for He is without need of the worlds. The judgments of originating or not originating are not separated here, though these relations may be spoken of from other standpoints. In this first respect existence is pure and undivided.

An objection immediately arises: does the expression 'He is existence' not predicate something distinct from its subject? Qūnawī's answer is that *existence* is used to convey the matter to understanding, since nothing is more universal in our concepts, not because a real name distinct from Him subsists at this rank. Suppose one did posit a name: it could not here be differentiated from the attribute, nor the attribute from the Essence. They are identical with sheer existence under this consideration. [The following page addresses divine perfections.]

title: Essential perfection and knowledge of all things by self-knowledge
speaker_layer: Qūnawī primary lemmata and al-Mahāʾimī commentary — working English translation
editorial_note: Working first-pass English from online Arabic transcription; source Arabic has not been embedded or critically collated.

pairs.en:
**Qūnawī:** “His perfection is His very essential existence, established by Himself and not by another. His life and power are identical with His knowledge, and His eternal knowledge of things is identical with His knowledge of Himself: He knows Himself by Himself and knows every thing by the very knowledge by which He knows Himself.”

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** This concerns the perfection attributed to the rank of *aḥadiyya* and the first determination. Perfection, as opposed to privation and nonbeing, belongs to existence; since the Real's existence is His own reality, His perfection is not obtained from something additional to Him. Were existence obtained from something distinct from existence, it could not be necessary through itself. His life and power likewise are not separately existing constituents of His reality. Life implies awareness of oneself, and power the realization of what He wills, in accordance with knowledge. The commentary likewise relates willing, hearing, seeing and speech to knowledge under this consideration.

There remains the difficulty of knowing the diverse things. His knowledge of Himself is not by an additional likeness or representative image, for then a second knowledge would be needed. All things, considered in the eternal rank, are existence and the intelligible realities: existence is His own reality, while the realities are the determinate forms of knowledge. Such forms do not stand apart from knowledge in the eternal rank. Qūnawī therefore says *eternally*: what is many in manifestation is not an independently multiple aggregate within essential knowledge. No differentiated accident or attribute has been introduced into the first rank.

**Qūnawī:** “In Him the different things are united, and from Him the many come forth, without containing Him or His containing them; without bringing Him forth from an earlier concealment, or His producing them from Himself. He has a unity that is the source of every multiplicity and a simplicity that is the very ground of every composition; He is last and first. What is contradictory in another is established for Him in the most perfect manner.”

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Different quiddities share existence; their plurality derives from its unitary root. But their emergence does not make them accidents lodged *within* God, or make Him a quality or occupant *within* them. [The exposition continues on p. 214.]

title: Unity as source, not receptacle, of multiplicity
speaker_layer: Qūnawī primary lemmata and al-Mahāʾimī commentary — working English translation
editorial_note: Working first-pass English from online Arabic transcription; source Arabic has not been embedded or critically collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The many realities are manifestations of the Real and manifested through Him. They do not disclose a Being who had previously been hidden from Himself: He has always been manifest to Himself. Any prior concealment is only relative to the created loci, before His appearance to them. Nor are those realities expelled from the divine Essence as bodies are displaced from a container. The fixed entities remain as they are: in themselves they do not acquire independent existence, though existence is displayed in and through their forms. Were they independent bearers to which existence subsequently attached as an accident, they would precede that existence, contrary to the argument.

How then can there be indefinitely many relations without compromising real unity or simplicity? The unity of the Real is the source of their multiplicity. These relations are contained there potentially—not as presently distinct parts, but by way of the analogy of a tree virtually contained in a seed. Considered in itself, the source is one in actuality; considered as the source of multiplicity, it contains the multiplicity virtually. Similarly, essential simplicity is the root of all combinations without itself being composed.

Qūnawī's first/last formulation therefore concerns two aspects: primordial unity and simplicity, and the posterior unfolding of their effects through manifestation. Yet this must not imply that a deficiency, temporal addition, or contingent composition enters the necessary, eternal Essence. Whatever features seem contrary to necessity are being attributed under an aspect of their relation to necessary existence, not under the aspect of the privation or nonbeing found in creation. Every qualified thing bears a relation to the unqualified; each manifestation expresses the Real in accordance with the receptivity of its locus. The text cautions readers against understanding its paradoxical expressions in a crudely literal way.

title: Opposites under distinct respects; not *ḥulūl* or *ittiḥād*
speaker_layer: Qūnawī primary lemmata and al-Mahāʾimī commentary — working English translation
editorial_note: Working first-pass English from online Arabic transcription; source Arabic has not been embedded or critically collated.

pairs.en:
**Qūnawī:** “Whoever speaks about Him *from himself* rather than *through Him*, denies of Him everything that perplexes him, and confines Him to what he can apprehend, is dumb and silent, ignorant and deceptive—until he beholds each opposite in the very reality of its opposite, indeed as identical with it, while still distinguishing its [created] reality from Him.”

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** This rebukes the thinker who assumes that he can distinguish the divine completely by the limits of his own understanding and therefore rejects whatever seems contrary to his concept of necessary being. He fails to discern that the reality of existence belongs to the Real while the independently existent 'other' he imagines is a reality which, in itself, has no such existence. To perceive both the eternal in the temporal and the temporal in the eternal, the necessary in the possible and the possible in the necessary, is not to assert that created substances dwell as parts in the divine Essence. It is to see the unity of existence while preserving distinctions of reality and respect. The commentator expressly rejects an inference to **indwelling (*ḥulūl*) or the merger of two independent existents (*ittiḥād*)**.

**Qūnawī:** “His unity is His multiplicity, His simplicity is His composition, His appearance is His concealment, His lastness is His firstness. He is not confined to a concept of unity or existence ...”

**Textual warning:** The online transcription at the transition after this last lemma inserts a lengthy passage repeating the discussion of the One and the effusion of common existence from earlier pages. It appears to be a conflated running lemma/editorial insertion, and cannot safely be printed as an uninterrupted Qūnawī quotation without comparison with the physical edition. The last line of this page is continuous with the next page's phrase “no witness / no witnessed object”. The translation therefore **does not silently harmonize the intrusive text**; the established continuation resumes on p. 216.

title: Unity and multiplicity without confinement to concepts
speaker_layer: Qūnawī primary lemmata and al-Mahāʾimī commentary — working English translation
editorial_note: Working first-pass English from online Arabic transcription; source Arabic has not been embedded or critically collated.

pairs.en:
**Qūnawī (continuation):** “... [He is not confined] to a witness or to what is witnessed. He may be as He has said and appear as He wills, without being restricted to absoluteness or qualification. To Him belongs the meaning encompassing every letter and the perfection comprehending every description. Whatever beauty remains hidden from those who are veiled, so that they imagine blemish or deficiency, when its inner reality is unveiled and the correctness of its attribution to Him is perceived, it assumes the form of perfection and is seen as a place of manifestation for majesty or beauty. All names and attributes, multiple within His very unity, are His own [under that aspect]. He does not disclaim what truly belongs to Him, nor does He conceal Himself from what He has manifested to perfect it.”

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The unity of existence and the multiplicity of its forms are not two opposed portions of one composed subject. Multiplicity pertains to the forms of its manifestation; without existence those forms are in themselves non-existent. Under the aspect of actual existence they share unity. Simplicity and composition, appearance and concealment, and firstness and lastness are likewise predicated under differing relations of source and manifestation. This does not mean that absolutely contradictory predicates hold of one restricted thing in precisely the same respect. The Real cannot be exhausted by any such restricted concept, whether 'unity' set over against multiplicity or 'existence' set over against an independently subsisting nonbeing.

He thus has no opposite or peer. Rational inference may establish necessary unity and existence, but it does not contain the Real within the concepts by which it argues. The experience of disclosure also cannot confine Him within the many particular manifestations it witnesses. He is as He says He is, and appears according to the eternally known receptivities of the fixed entities, in specified times and places; nevertheless neither undifferentiated *aḥadiyya* nor the articulated *wāḥidiyya* contains Him as a finite limit. [The remaining explanation begins on p. 217.]

title: Every manifestation receives the beauty and majesty appropriate to it
speaker_layer: Qūnawī primary lemmata and al-Mahāʾimī commentary — working English translation
editorial_note: Working first-pass English from online Arabic transcription; source Arabic has not been embedded or critically collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** The divine meaning embraces every ‘letter’ among necessary and possible things, and divine perfection comprehends every description, whether unqualified or qualified. Qūnawī next answers a difficulty. Created and qualified realities appear to be marked by blemish or privation; how can these be ascribed to that which is perfection itself? The apparent defect is a consequence of not seeing the inward beauty belonging to the disclosure of majesty and beauty. Once the underlying reality is disclosed, so that one understands in what respect existence can rightly be ascribed to it, one finds a form of existential perfection. It manifests as much as the receptivity of its locus permits and remains concealed in respect of what that locus cannot manifest. The limitations of the locus do not prevent it from being a place of manifestation for the divine names of majesty or beauty; on the contrary, the existence that is manifest in it is the most immediate indication of that disclosure.

Having argued that multiplicity is one with unity under the aspect of existence, Qūnawī must also explain the multiplicity of names and attributes. Their meanings and their characteristic effects differ, but under the consideration of what they truly predicate of the Real they belong to the one divine reality. To admit many predications is not to posit many gods. The plurality is attributed to names and attributes, not to several independently subsisting divine subjects. Al-Mahāʾimī compares this with the Sunni theological affirmation of attributes while rejecting a plurality of deities.

Nor need an experience of the attributes permanently veil the Essence. A seeker may first receive disclosures through the divine attributes and then, upon reaching completeness, receive disclosure of the Essence. For the complete one, a disclosure of one aspect does not conceal every other: even creation does not necessarily veil the Real, much less do the Real's own attributes. This leads to a further problem about describing the divine veil, majesty, self-sufficiency and transcendence while also attributing manifestation and relational nearness to Him.

title: Veil, majesty, sufficiency and holiness under distinct considerations
speaker_layer: Qūnawī primary lemmata and al-Mahāʾimī commentary — working English translation
editorial_note: Working first-pass English from online Arabic transcription; source Arabic has not been embedded or critically collated.

pairs.en:
**Qūnawī:** “His veil, majesty, self-sufficiency and holiness mean that His reality is distinct from everything opposed to it; that He does not depend upon another or require it for the establishment and permanence of His existence. Nothing, whether by itself or through another, is established except through Him. So take heed.”

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** ‘Veil’ here means that the divine reality is distinct from what would contradict it. The distinction produces an epistemic distance: one is unable to define the ultimate reality. If asked whether this posits a quiddity distinct from existence in God, the answer is no. One means the very **reality of existence through which existence is existence**. Existence is the most manifest thing with respect to the *that-it-is* (*anniyya*), yet in its essence it is most hidden, for no definition by genus and difference or by characteristic mark can comprehend it.

His majesty or inaccessibility (*ʿizza*) means that He is essentially unbound by another. Dependence upon what is lower would compromise the absolute standpoint. Under another consideration, however, His self-disclosure is related to the cosmos, which manifests and receives its existence thereby. His wealth (*ghināʾ*) means that His own existence and persistence need nothing else. Yet the manifestation of the divine names **as names manifest through loci** has a relation to the fixed entities in which they are displayed. His holiness (*quds*) collects the preceding senses: absolute independence and immunity from externally imposed deficiency under the aspect of the Essence, without denying the relations of disclosure under the aspect of the names. Everything that is actual exists only through Him; there is no independent existent forever concealed from Him, nor independent existent that compels Him to need it. Hence Qūnawī's warning to pay attention to the standpoint each predicate expresses.

**Qūnawī:** “Neither intellects nor thoughts apprehend Him under this respect; neither directions nor regions contain Him; neither inner sights nor outward eyes encompass His witnessing or knowledge. He is above corporeal and intelligible restrictions, immune to every estimate of quantity and quality, exalted beyond the encompassment of intuition, understanding, conjecture and knowledge, and concealed by the perfection of His majesty from all His creatures, perfect and imperfect.”

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Qūnawī now resumes the properties of existence merely as existence. No faculty of intellect, reflection, sensory sight, imaginal apprehension or inner witnessing can circumscribe it. [Continuation on p. 219.]

title: Limits of rational negations and the source of eternal knowledge
speaker_layer: Qūnawī primary lemmata and al-Mahāʾimī commentary — working English translation
editorial_note: Working first-pass English from online Arabic transcription; source Arabic has not been embedded or critically collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** Neither self-evident intellection nor discursive reasoning grasps Him as mere existence. Neither spatial regions and directions nor inward insight and outward seeing can encompass Him. Sense and thought apprehend qualified objects, whereas the Real is above formal and conceptual qualification. In relation to sensible things He is above estimations of amount, shape and quality; in relation to intellectual objects He is above the boundaries of intuitive, conceptual, conjectural and demonstrative comprehension. His own majesty veils Him from both the spiritually advanced person, who believes himself to approach through inner vision, and the person who turns away and remains at the level of outward sight. Qūnawī's qualification “as he thinks” for the one approaching stresses that even an authentic spiritual station does not constitute comprehensive apprehension of the unqualified Reality.

An objection now arises: if intellects cannot comprehend Him, are they not at least able to apprehend *that He is transcendent*? Qūnawī responds by distinguishing negative predication from affirmative, comprehensive acquaintance.

**Qūnawī:** “All the transcendences affirmed by intellects, whether by their thoughts or their inner insights, are negative judgments. They yield no real knowledge [of Him] and nevertheless fall short of what His majesty entails and His holiness and perfection deserve. The source of His knowledge's relation to the world is His very knowledge of Himself, and this relation appears through the appearance of the relations of His knowledge, which are His known things. He knows what is without limit both by the encompassment of His knowledge and by being the source of everything. Thus He knows His Essence, what is entailed by His Essence, and what is entailed by that entailment, collectively and individually, generally and in detail, and so without limit. What He determines—or knows to become determined in rank with a condition or cause—He knows together with its condition, cause, and consequence, having known its determination beforehand. Otherwise He knows it through Himself and as He wills. Yet no knowledge is renewed for Him, nor does any object or judgment become a limit confining Him.”

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Since the divine reality is existence, under that aspect it is not separated from the existents; His knowledge of Himself includes their source without becoming a collection of newly acquired images. The manifestation of relations of knowledge is the manifestation of the things known, just as the relation of existence to them becomes outwardly manifest through the known realities. [The argument is further resolved on p. 220.]

title: One knowledge comprehending infinite distinct things
speaker_layer: Qūnawī primary lemmata and al-Mahāʾimī commentary — working English translation
editorial_note: Working first-pass English from online Arabic transcription; source Arabic has not been embedded or critically collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The difficulty is that one essential knowledge seems unable to comprehend the infinitely many differentiated objects of knowledge. It does so from two aspects. First, the divine knowledge encompasses the Essence, and the realities of things are its intrinsic affairs (*shuʾūn*); the inclusion of these realities is not an additional cognition appended from without. Second, insofar as things are manifested, the Real is their originating source. Sourcehood is among the essential perfections and is therefore intelligible through knowledge of the Essence. Knowing the ground entails knowing what belongs to that ground, and knowing a necessary concomitant entails knowing the consequences flowing from it. The Real therefore knows His sourcehood and the relation of manifestation to the realities, which are intrinsic affairs considered in the Essence and fixed entities considered in the rank of knowledge. He knows them in collection and summary under one consideration; individually and in detail through their relations and determined effects under another. Thus a single essential knowledge encompasses indefinitely many things.

Yet a further difficulty remains concerning temporal contingencies. A particular event may depend upon an external condition or cause and thus seem not to be a necessary concomitant of the divine Essence. Qūnawī answers that what is determined to occur through a given condition or cause is known *as so conditioned*. He knows the rank of each thing and the circumstances under which it comes to manifestation, without His own Essence or essential knowing depending upon a temporal external prerequisite. The condition and cause ultimately have an intelligible relation to what proceeds from His sourcehood, although the occurrence of the thing is contingent.

If the occurrence is through a necessary concomitant, knowledge of the consequent is contained in knowledge of the ground; if a condition and cause are involved, their order is also eternally known. If no such condition or cause intervenes, the thing is known through the divine sourcehood directly and is manifested as He wills. In each case the order is known without a newly acquired act of knowing. [The argument concerning time is developed on p. 221.]

title: Temporal succession does not imply renewed divine knowledge
speaker_layer: Qūnawī primary lemmata and al-Mahāʾimī commentary — working English translation
editorial_note: Working first-pass English from online Arabic transcription; source Arabic has not been embedded or critically collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī:** One might suppose that if God knows a thing through its cause, condition and concomitants, His knowledge must change as these occur. Suppose He knows eternally that Zayd will exist at a certain time; when Zayd appears, what was future seems present, and when Zayd passes away, it seems past. But the one eternal knowledge encompasses Zayd's existence at that particular time, the temporal present relative to that time, its futurity relative to an earlier point, and its pastness relative to a later one. These relations belong to the ordered object known and do not require successive new knowledge in the Knower.

The same is true of a thing's dependence on a cause or condition: God eternally knows the ordered dependence, rather than first knowing the condition and then, at a later time, acquiring knowledge of what it conditions. New knowledge would arise in a knower whose own situation is bounded by a changing temporal standpoint. Since the Real is not confined to the divisions of time, no new temporal relation is added to His knowledge when a thing comes to pass. He knows all the object's aspects by one eternal knowledge. Even the changing knowledge of created knowers is intelligible under His knowledge, which is the source from which their knowledge proceeds. Qūnawī invokes the Qurʾānic formulation “until We know” (Q 47:31): the renewal concerns manifestation and differentiation in the created loci, not an increase in the essential divine knowledge.

**Qūnawī:** “His perfection is through Himself; His existence is actual and not potential, necessary and not possible. He is exalted above familiar change and origination. Generated things do not contain Him, whether to display or to shelter Him; He does not form them because He needs another, nor do they constitute Him. Things are connected with Him insofar as the determinations proceed from Him, but He is not connected with them insofar as their multiplicity differentiates them from Him. Their existence depends upon Him and His does not depend upon them. By His reality He has no need of anything; everything in its existence needs Him.”

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The perfection at issue is intrinsic, not a product of the names, attributes or manifestations considered as additions to the divine Essence. The outward manifestation reflects that intrinsic perfection, as a reflection depends on the luminous original without augmenting it. [Continuation on p. 222.]

title: Intrinsic necessity and relational manifestation
speaker_layer: Qūnawī primary lemmata and al-Mahāʾimī commentary — working English translation
editorial_note: Working first-pass English from online Arabic transcription; source Arabic has not been embedded or critically collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The Real's existence is always actual. Potentiality implies an unfulfilled possibility and hence a deficiency; such potentiality cannot belong to His existence in itself, although relations of action and loci of manifestation involve possibilities whose actualization is determined. In Himself He exists necessarily, whereas the appearance of things in their particular loci is contingent. Because His necessity admits no replacement of one intrinsic state by another, He is above change. His relations to successive loci can differ without the Essence becoming an accidental subject in which changes occur.

Neither is He contained by originated things as a colour inheres in a coloured body, or a spatial substance in a receptacle; nor is He enclosed to preserve Him from being manifest. Such containment would introduce intrinsic dependence and would confuse His manifestation through the loci with His self-manifestation to Himself. He does not create temporal existents to repair a deficiency or satisfy a need. Their manifestation concerns the outward disclosure of the possible affairs and capacities comprised within the divine knowledge, not a new essential perfection acquired from what was previously absent. Nor do the generated things create or constitute Him, since His own existence is necessary and does not occur twice. It is they whose properties become outwardly actual through His relation to them.

Why then are things related to Him at all, if He does not need them? The relation pertains to their dependence upon His existence and to their own determinate manifestation, not to a need in Him. It is not because they possess independent existence as a second kind of being; their plurality comes from their differing realities, while the existence they receive is one as effusion. They depend upon that existence, which depends on none of them. In Himself He is without need; every possible thing lacks existence of its own. Otherwise all possible things would be necessary through themselves, and the number of independently eternal necessaries would multiply.

title: Divine care is the effusion of existential light
speaker_layer: Qūnawī primary lemmata and al-Mahāʾimī commentary — working English translation
editorial_note: Working first-pass English from online Arabic transcription; source Arabic has not been embedded or critically collated.

pairs.en:
**Qūnawī:** “Between Him and things there is no relation save providential care (*ʿināya*), as has been said; and no veil except ignorance, confusion and imagination arising from the utmost closeness of His nearness and the excess of His majesty and exaltedness. In reality His providential care is the effusion of His existential light upon what is inscribed in the mirror of its fixed entity, the relation of its knownness [to Him], and is prepared to receive the ruling of His bringing it into existence and displaying Himself through it. ‘There is nothing like Him’ from the first aspect, and ‘He is the Hearing, the Seeing’ from the second.”

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Qūnawī now explicitly enters the second consideration of existence, although the previous account of existence in itself had to discuss relation by way of preparation. Since the Real is intrinsically without need, the relation of existents to Him cannot mean that the Essence is improved by them. The philosophers have termed the governing relation *providential care*, understood as the prior knowledge by which the order of the world is established. Yet knowledge of them alone would not produce outward actuality without manifestation. Thus, in its fullest sense, providential care is the effusion of existential light: the determination of existence under its illuminating, manifesting aspect rather than as an addition to the Essence itself.

There is no veil separating creatures from the Real as an independently existent obstruction. Their veiling arises from their ignorance and their imagining many independent existences where the plurality belongs instead to the determinations in which one existence is displayed. The Real's intimacy is too great and His majesty too exalted for any single locus to comprehend Him.

The recipient of this effusion is not the fixed entity in itself, since it remains non-existent in the sense already established. Rather, it is the determinate form disclosed in the mirror of that entity; its determinate relation to eternal knowledge provides the respect under which it is capable of manifestation. Only what is prepared to receive the divine ruling of manifestation actually appears; a thing's abstract possibility alone does not require its actual existence. The verse “There is nothing like Him, and He is the Hearing, the Seeing” (Q 42:11) is read according to the two considerations: uncompromising transcendence in the first, divine manifestation under the names in the second. [The detailed explanation continues on p. 224.]


### Scholarly notes

1. **One knowledge and temporal relations:** a crucial distinction between the eternal order of the known and a temporal change in the Knower. The text cannot be reduced to a claim that God knows only universals; particular times and conditions are included.
2. **Negation versus experiential knowledge:** the insufficiency of negative theology is not a rejection of rational proof as false; it rejects negations as adequate *exhaustive* knowledge of the divine Reality.
3. ***ʿInāya*:** the rendering “providential care” covers a philosophical term whose sense Qūnawī reworks as the positive effusion of existential manifestation, not merely God's cognitive planning.
4. **Distinct considerations:** language that unites opposites is consistently governed by distinct levels of attribution. The text does not license contradictions in a single, unqualified respect.
5. **Textual status:** Modern printed footnotes have not been silently incorporated into the translated medieval running text. Reported narrations and scriptural citations have not been individually authenticated here.

**Next page:** 224, continuing the contrast between intellectual transcendence and the hearing/seeing of divine manifestation.

title: The Real apprehended only under the relation of manifestation
speaker_layer: Qūnawī primary lemmata and al-Mahāʾimī commentary — working English translation
editorial_note: Working first-pass English from online Arabic transcription; source Arabic has not been embedded or critically collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** In His unqualified aspect there is no other existence that might be His like; this accounts for the denial of likeness in the first part of the Qurʾānic verse. Hearing and sight belong to the second aspect, in which the divine names are made manifest. Even here there is a form of transcendence known by unveiling, when the divine names are understood without making any created locus independently divine. Qūnawī indicates that transcendence persists, notwithstanding every manifestation.

**Qūnawī:** “Whenever He is apprehended or witnessed, or addresses or is addressed, it is from behind the veil of His majesty in the rank of Himself already mentioned, by virtue of the relation of His manifestness and the ruling of His self-disclosure in the station of His drawing near: that is, the association of His universal existence with the possibilities and the dawning of His light upon the entities of existents; nothing besides this.”

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Whether the Real is apprehended in certain knowledge, witnessed in a realized disclosure, addresses an angel, prophet or saint, or is addressed by such a person, His unqualified reality remains behind the veil of majesty in the rank of unity (*aḥadiyya*). He is not thereby brought within the definition or comprehension of a creature. These forms of apprehension and address concern the relation by which He is outwardly manifest to things. Their reality is a self-disclosure in the station of descending nearness. “Association” (*iqtirān*) does not signify spatial joining or contact: His light shines upon the entities that are its loci of manifestation. The original transcendence remains intact. Qūnawī next explains why what is outwardly called the world is nonetheless referred to as other than the Real.

**Qūnawī:** “Under this aspect, when the determination of His existence is considered as bound by the attributes necessary to each determined possible entity—which, collectively and severally, are in reality the relations of His knowledge—and by whatever accompanies these attributes of affairs, peculiar properties and accidents, and by the effects of the rulings of the Name *Time* (*al-Dahr*), called times, ranks and locations, this determination and individuation is called creation and ‘other’; you will shortly learn its secret, God willing.”

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Only the existence considered as determined by the attributes of possible entities is called created or ‘other’. Such designation does not apply to unqualified existence in itself, nor simply to its divine and lordly determinations. Impossible things are excluded: they are not a created locus merely by being conceived. The specific constitutive attributes of possibility are the respect under which the created order is distinguished. [The exposition continues on p. 225.]

title: Fixed entities, constitutive properties, adventitious states and time
speaker_layer: Qūnawī primary lemmata and al-Mahāʾimī commentary — working English translation
editorial_note: Working first-pass English from online Arabic transcription; source Arabic has not been embedded or critically collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Qūnawī calls the determinate entities relations of divine knowledge to signal that, in themselves, they do not possess a positive independent existence. Their essential attributes cannot supply another kind of existence over against the Real; rather, existence is considered as determined by those attributes. He explicitly says “collectively and severally,” lest anyone think that a combination of properties must belong only to divinity, or conversely that a determinate possible entity ceases to be a created thing once considered in a collection. The collection at issue is the aggregate of properties consequent upon determinate manifestation in possible entities, not the divine comprehensive unity as such.

The accompanying characteristics make the created standpoint more explicit. Qūnawī includes the entities' *shuʾūn*, that is, their capacities to bear existential qualities; their peculiarities, which distinguish one sort of thing from another; and accidents which attach without being peculiar to their subjects. The distinctive characteristics of a locus are not all merely temporary. Some persist with the subject despite not being among its primary constitutive attributes. The effects of the divine name *al-Dahr*—Time—are likewise introduced. Al-Mahāʾimī refers to the prophetic report in which God says, in substance, that the human being abuses Time whereas God disposes night and day. The effects called times involve temporal changes; those arising through ranks involve higher and lower worlds; those through stations or locations involve such processes as the elements receiving composition and alteration from one form to another.

This enumeration is not designed to leave some created things outside the definition. It gathers the sorts of determination through which createdness and its properties are properly understood, whether the effects are essential, distinctive, adventitious, temporal, positional or configurational. Qūnawī promises to explain their basis by the pervasion of the existential light. First he gives the rulings of existence in its conditioned aspect.

**Qūnawī (opening the next lemma):** “At that point every description is attributed to it…” [Continuation on p. 226.]

title: Attributing created predicates to existence under its determinations
speaker_layer: Qūnawī primary lemmata and al-Mahāʾimī commentary — working English translation
editorial_note: Working first-pass English from online Arabic transcription; source Arabic has not been embedded or critically collated.

pairs.en:
**Qūnawī (continuing):** “…it is called by every name, appears under every description, receives every ruling, is determined in every place by whatever description belongs there, and is apprehended through every perceptive faculty—sight, hearing, intellect, understanding and other powers of perception. So recollect!”

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** When existence is considered under the determinations described above, every originated description is attributed to it from that perspective, not to the absolute Essence under the same aspect. It is named with the names of originated things and displayed with their marks. It receives the rulings of the changes belonging to those things. In every place—whether a sensible place or an intelligible station—it is described in the way proper to that locus. And it is known through the faculty appropriate to the manifestation: through hearing and seeing outwardly, or through intellect, understanding, common sense, imagination, estimation, memory, reflection, soul, heart and spirit inwardly. Remember the distinction, lest the Real veil you from creation or creation veil you from the Real.

**Qūnawī:** “Know that this occurs through His pervasion of everything with His essential light, holy above division, partition and indwelling in spirits and bodies. Understand! Yet all this is whenever He loves and however He wills.”

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The predication is intelligible because His light is manifest throughout things, not because a part of His substance departs and passes into another substance. This is the essential light of existence by which everything is made manifest; in itself it cannot be cut into portions according to the number of mirrors or loci. Each manifestation is displayed according to the receptivity granted to it. Pervasion (*sarayān*) therefore does **not** mean *ḥulūl*, whether an indwelling in incorporeal spirits or a bodily inherence. Nor is manifestation compelled by an intrinsic necessity arising out of the creatures' capacities. Their receptivity itself depends on divine love and will; He manifests as and when He wills, in accordance with the readiness He bestows. What is conditioned by particular forms belongs to the standpoint of this manifestation, not to the Essence as an independent alteration.

**Qūnawī (next lemma):** “At every time and in every state He is, through Himself and not through anything added, receptive to the two opposed universal rulings already mentioned, and comprehends every pair of differing things, absent and present, departing and arriving. If He wills, He appears in every form; if He does not will, no form is attributed to Him.” [Commentary continues on p. 227.]

title: Absolute and conditioned: two standpoints, not two divine substances
speaker_layer: Qūnawī primary lemmata and al-Mahāʾimī commentary — working English translation
editorial_note: Working first-pass English from online Arabic transcription; source Arabic has not been embedded or critically collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The two comprehensive rulings are non-determination and determination: considered in Himself, He is abstracted from every form; considered in the relation of manifestation, He appears under the terms of every kind of form. These are opposed as descriptions of the determinate individual subject. To speak of His being receptive to both “through Himself” does not posit some additional thing to which absolute existence could be attached. There is nothing beyond unqualified existence that could supply a second ontological constituent. The factors under which manifestation is considered are additional only at the level of respect or consideration (*iʿtibār*), not independent existential components.

Nor is the phrase “at every time” to be projected backwards as though all temporal events had been eternally actual. Such a projection would make originated things without beginning. The eternal standpoint remains different from the temporally determined one. The Real comprehends not merely strictly opposed descriptions but every variety of difference, through the forms in which the determinations appear. Forms differ according to what is manifested in them, and the determinate appearance of each depends on will. Thus, if He wills to manifest, a given form appears; without such determination there is no created form attributed under this aspect. At the final proclamation “To whom belongs dominion today? To God, the One, the Overpowering” (Q 40:16), the matter is exemplified by the disappearance of those appearances.

The unmanifested form is not an instance of divine will itself ceasing to be eternal. What ceases, or does not obtain, is the relation of will to a particular appearance. Qūnawī therefore stresses that the differing forms do not compromise what the Real eternally is in unity.

**Qūnawī:** “Neither His determination and individuation by forms nor His being described by their properties impair the perfection of His existence, His majesty or His holiness. His appearing within things, manifesting them, and being determined and conditioned by them and their rulings under that aspect do not contradict His exaltedness and unconditioned freedom from restrictions, or His independence of everything described as existent. Rather, He unites realities that resemble or differ [within a field of affinity], so that they are brought together, and those that are unlike or distinct, so that they remain different.”

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Specific and individual determinations concern the loci, not an intrinsic accident newly acquired by divine being. The example is the image in a mirror: when a mirror is shaken or broken, the change belongs to the reflected image, not the original whose image it bears. Thus emergence of differences in the places of manifestation cannot break absolute freedom from limitation, diminish necessity or introduce real accidents into the Essence. [Continuation on p. 228.]

title: Affinity, difference, expansion and contraction
speaker_layer: Qūnawī primary lemmata and al-Mahāʾimī commentary — working English translation
editorial_note: Working first-pass English from online Arabic transcription; source Arabic has not been embedded or critically collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** His exaltedness and essential independence remain as they were. Yet His manifestation also gathers realities that resemble one another and others that, though different, stand in some affinity. Such things may be joined in a unity proportionate to their relationship. By contrast, other realities are mutually contrary or so unlike that there is no specific affinity by which they would form a single determinate class; these remain different. Nevertheless they too are gathered in existence, since all appear through its light. The union and separation belong to the expression of their capacities under the one encompassing existence.

**Qūnawī:** “Through His existential self-disclosure hidden things appeared, and blessings descended from the unseen into witnessing, by virtue of His names *al-Bāsiṭ* (the Expander) and *al-Mubdiʾ* (the Originator). With the lifting of the ruling of His drawing near, existents are hidden and become non-existent, by virtue of His names *al-Qābiḍ* (the Contracter) and *al-Muʿīd* (the Restorer).”

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The name Expander is expressed by the spreading of universal existence across determinate realities; Originator is expressed by their outward manifestation together with their properties and states. Thus the realities and their attributes previously concealed in the rank of unified knowledge become manifest. Blessings descend from the unseen rank of unity to external witnessing, actualizing what was formerly only potential with respect to their outward appearance. When the ruling of intimate existential disclosure is lifted, outward actuality disappears: what had appeared is concealed or becomes externally non-existent. This is related to the names Contracter and Restorer, whereby the manifested thing returns to its previous unmanifest state. These statements concern the changing determinations of manifestation, not a change in the eternal existence or a transfer of the divine Essence from place to place.

**Qūnawī:** “He was veiled by His majesty and was *Ghafūr* (the Concealer); if He loved to be known, He drew near and appeared in whatever He willed, however He willed, and was *Wadūd* (the Loving). Through love, as the Lover, He brings forth; love manifests Him. Through it, as both Lover and Beloved, He restores everything, [everything being] in His grasp and subdued beneath the strength of His power, because of the strength of His acting and the weakness of that which receives the action.”

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Concealment in majesty is considered as the Real's exaltedness and independence. Love of being known is considered as the manifestation of latent possibilities and the fulfillment of the world through loci of disclosure, by eternal will. The name *Wadūd* describes His manifesting and being manifested. As Lover He originates, since before creation there is no created beloved in external existence; as Lover and Beloved He also draws back what was manifested. [Continues on p. 229.]

title: Love, return and the ‘glorious Throne’ as an intermediary
speaker_layer: Qūnawī primary lemmata and al-Mahāʾimī commentary — working English translation
editorial_note: Working first-pass English from online Arabic transcription; source Arabic has not been embedded or critically collated.

pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** Through love under the aspect of being the Lover, He brings things to outward existence, and He is thereby disclosed in them, although He is already manifest to Himself in Himself. As Lover in created forms and as Beloved under the aspect of reality, He causes things to return to Him. Al-Mahāʾimī adduces the saying “Love of one's homeland is part of faith” to illustrate this return. **Critical note:** this saying is not thereby established as an authentic prophetic ḥadīth; its attribution requires separate verification.

Love and being beloved are not, by themselves, sufficient to account for creation and return. Every thing remains within the grasp of divine will and beneath His irresistible power. The decisive difference is between the strength of the agent and the weakness of what receives the action. The former is active and encompassing; the latter passive and subjected to the ruling. No created intermediary therefore becomes another independent originating agent, and the Real does not become a passive subject constituted by what proceeds from Him.

**Qūnawī:** “The locus of the manifestation of His power, the instrument of His wisdom in acting according to His practice, the site of the disclosure of the secret of contraction and expansion, origination and concealment, unseen and seen, unveiling and the formal causal veil by which He carries out what has been described—though not absolutely—is His glorious Throne.”

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** He interprets the “glorious Throne” here as the First Intellect, appealing to a treatise attributed to Ibn ʿArabī. It is the locus where the divine irresistible power becomes perceptible within the patterned order of causes and effects, while the law of the ordered cosmos proceeds through the orientations of universal intellects and souls. The First Intellect can be described under both aspects: possibility and dependence in itself, necessity through its Lord; emergence into existence and abstraction from sensible extension; belonging to the unseen world and being manifested through God; inscription of intelligible realities and acting as a veil through its place between the Real and the created order. Its causality, however, must not be construed as independent efficient power. What happens takes place **upon** or **in conjunction with** the intermediary's orientation, rather than owing its ultimate origin to an agent other than God.

[ ولهذا قال سبحانه وتعالى مبدئ سر هذا الأمر : لِمَنْ كانَ لَهُ قَلْبٌ أَوْ أَلْقَى السَّمْعَ وَهُوَ شَهِيدٌ [ ق : 37 ] ، إِنَّ بَطْشَ رَبِّكَ لَشَدِيدٌ ( 12 ) إِنَّهُ هُوَ يُبْدِئُ وَيُعِيدُ ( 13 ) وَهُوَ الْغَفُورُ الْوَدُودُ ( 14 ) ذُو الْعَرْشِ الْمَجِيدُ ( 15 ) فَعَّالٌ لِما يُرِيدُ ( 16 ) [ البروج : 12 - 16 ] في مرتبتي الإطلاق والتقييد ، وقوله : فَعَّالٌ لِما يُرِيدُ [ البروج : 16 ] ، جواب سؤال مقدر ، علم أنه يبدو من معترض محجوب ] .

أي : لما ذكرنا من الترتيب ، قال سبحانه لإظهار سر هذا الترتيب بطريق الرمز بحيث يختص بالفهم من كان له قلب يستكشف المعاني الغامضة من القرآن ، أو ألقى السمع إلى المشايخ الكاشفة لها ، وهو حاضر كامل التوجه ، كأنه ينظر إلى ما يسمع أن بطش - أي قدرة - ربك لشديد يؤثر فيما شاء كيف شاء أنه هو يبدي من حيث كونه ودودا ، ويعيد من حيث كونه غفورا ودودا معا ، يفعل ذلك بالعرش المجيد الذي هو العقل الأول .

الإعادة إلى البطون ، والإبداء إلى الظهور ، في قوله تعالى : فَعَّالٌ لِما يُرِيدُ [ البروج : 16 ] ، إشارة إلى أنه لا يحتاج إلى الأسباب كما يتوهم من قوله تعالى : ذُو الْعَرْشِ الْمَجِيدُ [ البروج : 15 ] ، بل فَعَّالٌ لِما يُرِيدُ [ البروج : 16 ] ، بالأسباب وبدونها . وإنما الأسباب على مقتضى الحكمة ، وإلى أنه ليس موجبا بالذات ، كما يتوهم من أن الغفورية والودودية يوجبان الإعادة والإبداء ، فبيّن أن تجابيها أيضا بمشيئته واختياره لا بإيجاب ، كما يقول أهل الحجاب .

النص الثاني والعشرون : ولما فرغ عن تحقيق التوحد ، شرع في كشف ما يحجب عنه غالبا ، فذلك بما قال رضي اللّه عنه : [ نص شريف ] هو آخر النصوص ؛ لأن كمال إيضاح التوحيد الذي هو أشرف المطالب حاصل به ، والحجب الباقية تيسر انكشافه عند انكشافه وآخريته لأن كمال اتضاح التوحيد في مقام أحدية الجمع والفرق ، وهو آخر المقامات فيما يتعارف .

قال الشيخ رضي اللّه عنه : [ اعلم أن أعظم الشبه والحجب أن التعدّدات الواقعة في الوجود الواحد توجب آثار الأعيان الثابتة فيه ، فتوهم أن الأعيان ظهرت في الوجود وبالوجود ،
pairs.en:
**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** The Real creates at the occasion of the First Intellect's turning, not because that turning assists an otherwise deficient divine act. As with human actions in the theological account to which al-Mahāʾimī alludes, the creature's intention accompanies an act that is ultimately the creation of God. Causal order is the form in which divine wisdom is displayed, not an external necessity governing God.

**Qūnawī:** “For this reason He said, disclosing the secret of the matter: ‘For one who has a heart, or gives ear while present’ (Q 50:37); and: ‘Surely your Lord's grasp is mighty. It is He who originates and restores. He is the Forgiving, the Loving, Lord of the Glorious Throne, Doer of whatever He wills’ (Q 85:12–16), under the two ranks of absoluteness and determination. His saying, ‘Doer of whatever He wills,’ answers an anticipated objection, which He knew a veiled objector would raise.”

**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Qūnawī treats these verses as an allusive presentation of the preceding order. The one with a heart is capable of perceiving subtle Qurʾānic meanings; the one who listens with full attention receives teaching that discloses them. God's “grasp” points to irresistible power. Origination corresponds to bringing possibilities to manifestation, and restoration to their return to concealment; lovingness and forgiveness are read under these related standpoints. The glorious Throne symbolizes the First Intellect as a locus through which the wisdom of ordered effects is disclosed.

The anticipated objection arises because the reference to the Throne might make one think God requires the intermediary in order to act. Hence “Doer of whatever He wills”: He acts **with causes or without them**. Causes belong to wisdom and order, not to a necessity imposed on His ability. Likewise the divine names associated with love and concealment do not compel an emanation by the nature of a necessary mechanism. Their manifestation occurs through divine choosing and will. This closes al-Mahāʾimī's exposition of Text Twenty-One.
